On the wood of the cross, Jesus didn't just show compassion: He truly bore your debt in His body. Nothing sin required was left for you to pay. So receive the peace purchased at that price, and stop paying a debt that has already been paid in full.

Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me. — Psalms 23:4.

When trials strike, one thought almost always creeps in: “If God were here, this wouldn't be happening to me.” Suffering seems like proof of His absence. Yet Scripture says the opposite. The dark valley isn't the place where God disappears; it's often the very place where His presence is revealed most clearly.

The psalmist doesn't say, “I will never go through the valley of the shadow of death.” He says, “even though I walk” through that valley. The trial isn't avoided. But right in the heart of that darkness, he discovers a certainty: “You are with me.” It isn't in the green pastures that he proclaims God's presence; it's in the valley.

Often, that's exactly where God draws closest. Not because He loves our tears, but because it's when we're stripped bare that we stop leaning on ourselves and start leaning on Him. Many believers testify, “I've never felt God as much as I did in my darkest night.”

For you today: are you walking through a valley where you're tempted to believe God has slipped away? Read it differently. His presence isn't measured by the absence of difficulty, but by His promise: “I am with you.” Seek Him, not beyond the trial, but in the middle of it.

In the blazing furnace, Daniel's three friends were not alone: a fourth figure walked with them in the fire. God didn't spare them from the furnace; He went into it with them. He does the same for you. The trial doesn't prove His absence: it's often the place where you discover, more than ever, that He is there.

You number my wanderings; put my tears into Your bottle; are they not in Your book? — Psalms 56:8.

We sometimes think our tears are useless, lost, unseen. We cry alone at night and feel that this pain matters to no one, that it evaporates without a trace. The image the psalmist gives is deeply moving: God collects your tears “in His bottle,” He keeps them, He records them in His book. Not one is lost.

This means that nothing of your pain escapes God’s gaze. He doesn’t look away from your sorrow; He gathers it carefully, the way you keep something of great value. Your tears don’t fall into the void: they fall into His hands. And what is in God’s hands is never wasted.

For God doesn’t simply count your tears; He does something with them. What you have wept over, He can transform. Pain entrusted to His hands often becomes, later on, a source of compassion for others, a new depth, an unexpected fruit. Nothing you entrust to Him, not even your weeping, is lost to His work.

For you today: what sorrow are you carrying, thinking it matters to no one? Place it in God’s hands. Not so He can sweep it aside as if it didn’t exist, but because He sees it, gathers it, and will not waste it.

Mary Magdalene’s tears at the empty tomb were not ignored: it was to her, weeping, that the risen Lord first revealed Himself. God met her in her tears. He meets you in yours too. Not one of your tears placed in His hands is lost.

Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. — Galatians 6:7.

Nothing stays small for very long. What we tolerate in secret — a thought we entertain, a habit we excuse, a compromise we think has no consequences — grows in silence, hidden from view. We tell ourselves it's under control, that “it isn't hurting anyone.” But what you tolerate in private always ends up ruling you in public.

The law of sowing is relentless: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” God is not mocked, Paul says; no one cheats this law. The little seeds planted in the darkness of your heart don't stay in the ground: they grow, and one day they bear their fruit, visible to everyone.

This works both ways. The bad you sow in secret will one day steer your conduct in broad daylight. But the good you sow — faithful prayer, quiet obedience, thoughts kept pure — will also bear its fruit, in strength and in character. Tomorrow's harvest is decided by today's sowing.

For you today: what are you tolerating in secret, thinking it will have no effect? A grudge you keep feeding, a look you keep entertaining, a small dishonesty. Don't let it grow. Pull up the seed while it's still small, before it takes control of your visible life.

David first tolerated a look in secret; that tolerated look led him, from compromise to compromise, to a public and devastating fall. It all began with what no one could see. Guard your secret life: it is there, more than anywhere else, that the direction of your life is sown.

Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it spring the issues of life. — Proverbs 4:23.

Talent opens doors, draws attention, and helps you rise fast. A gift, a skill, or a charisma can lift you to places others take years to reach. But rising is not the same as standing. Talent can lift you up; only character can keep you at the height it carried you to. Many have risen by their gift and fallen by their heart.

That is why the Bible places the emphasis not first on abilities, but on the heart: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it spring the issues of life.” Who you are on the inside, in secret, determines whether you will be able to carry, over the long haul, what your talent has given you. Your gift puts you in the spotlight; your character keeps you standing.

We are tempted to work mostly on what can be seen: performance, image, results. And to neglect what cannot be seen: humility, integrity, faithfulness in the little things. But talent resting on fragile character is a magnificent house built on sand. Sooner or later, the storm reveals the foundations.

For you today: are you investing more in your skills than in your character? Take care of your heart first. Cultivate in secret what will keep you in the light: honesty, prayer, self-control, humility. These are the roots that will determine your stability.

Saul had the stature of a king; it was his heart that brought him down. David had no greater guarantees, but he had a heart that kept returning to God; that is what kept him. Talent may open great doors for you. Make sure your character is strong enough to keep you there.

Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. — 1 Corinthians 8:1.

It's easy to confuse spiritual maturity with how much you know. The person who knows lots of verses, who has read many books, who can discuss theology, would surely seem further along. But Paul warns: “knowledge puffs up.” It can inflate the ego without transforming the heart. True maturity isn't measured by what you know, but by who you become.

Knowing and becoming are two different things. You can know everything about love and still be hard; know all about forgiveness and still hold a grudge; master the doctrine of humility and be full of pride. Knowledge that stays in the head puffs up; love that flows down into your life builds up. The sign of maturity isn't the breadth of your knowledge, it's how much your character resembles Christ's.

This puts priorities back in order. The goal of what you learn is never accumulation, but transformation. A truth known but not lived doesn't make you more mature; it only makes you more accountable. Better a little knowledge put into practice than a great deal of learning that changes nothing.

For you today: do you measure your growth by what you know, or by who you are becoming? Take a truth you already know very well and ask yourself: am I living it? Choose today to become a little more like what you already know.

The Pharisees knew the Scriptures better than anyone; yet they missed the very One those Scriptures proclaimed. Their vast knowledge had not produced a transformed heart. Don't settle for knowing: let what you know shape you, because maturity is measured by who you become.

Be holy, for I am holy. — 1 Peter 1:16.

The word “holiness” often wrongly brings to mind an image of stiff perfection, a flawless facade, people who think they're better than everyone else. We picture an effort to look more virtuous, cleaner, more above it all. But in the Bible, being holy doesn't first mean “looking better”: it means “being set apart,” belonging wholly to God.

In the Old Testament, a holy object wasn't made of some superior material; it was an object reserved, consecrated for a special use, set apart for God. So holiness isn't a moral performance to put on display; it's a belonging to live out. “Be holy, for I am holy”: you are his, completely, and that is what changes the way you live.

This understanding sets you free from hypocrisy. Trying to look better produces facades; knowing you belong wholly to God produces real transformation. You no longer try to impress others with your virtue; you simply live as someone who belongs to Another, and that belonging shapes your choices, your words, your body, your time.

For you today: is your pursuit of holiness a matter of image—looking good—or of belonging—being God's? There may be an area of your life you haven't yet truly “set apart” for him. Offer it to him. Not to look better, but because you are his.

Daniel didn't try to impress the court of Babylon with his piety; he simply lived as someone who belonged to God, down to the details, even when it cost him. His holiness wasn't a facade; it was a belonging. May it be so for you: not looking better, but being wholly God's.

Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. — Galatians 5:16.

We imagine that freedom means doing whatever we want, without limits. But experience proves the opposite: the one who obeys every craving isn't free, he's a slave. A slave to his anger, his impulses, his appetites. True freedom isn't obeying your cravings: it's no longer being forced to obey them. That is self-control.

Self-control isn't a grim deprivation; it's a liberation. As long as your craving is in command, it's the master and you're the servant. When you can say no to a craving that is destroying you, you become free again. You're no longer driven by whatever passes through you; you choose, you decide, you lead your life instead of just enduring it.

But this freedom isn't won by sheer willpower and clenched fists. Paul gives the secret: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.” You don't win by fighting head-on against every craving; you win by walking under a different leading. You don't drive out darkness by brute force; you turn on the light.

For you today: what craving has a hold on you right now, to the point that you believe you can't say no to it? Don't settle for gritting your teeth. Ask the Spirit to lead you, step by step, and let His presence produce in you the freedom that willpower alone can never give.

Joseph, tempted in the prime of his youth, was able to say no and flee—not through some extraordinary moral strength, but because a greater presence held him: “How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” His self-control was freedom. Walk by the Spirit, and you too will discover the freedom to stop obeying your cravings.

Abide in Me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in Me. — John 15:4.

When we long to bear fruit — to be useful, fruitful, to see our lives count — our first reflex is to get busy. Do more, run faster, double our efforts. But Jesus points to a completely different way. Fruit doesn't come from frantic activity; it comes from connection. “Abide in Me.” Bearing fruit starts with abiding, not with striving.

The image of the branch is crystal clear. A branch doesn't produce grapes by straining and forcing; it bears fruit simply because it stays connected to the vine and the sap keeps flowing. Cut it off, leave it to strain on its own, and it withers. “The branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine.” The secret isn't effort; it's connection.

This sets you free from an exhausting religion. You don't have to produce fruit in your own strength, as if everything depended on how hard you push. Your first job isn't to manufacture, but to stay connected. Abide in Christ — in prayer, in His Word, in His presence — and the sap will do its work in you, naturally, without strain.

For you today: are you trying to bear fruit by striving, or by abiding? Maybe God is inviting you not so much to do more, but to stay more deeply connected to Him. Slow down. Come back to the vine. Let the life of Christ flow through you before you try to produce anything at all.

Mary, sitting at Jesus' feet, seemed to be “doing nothing” while Martha bustled about. Yet she was the one who had chosen the good part. True fruit will always grow from that place: not from frantic activity, but from abiding presence with Him. Abide, and the fruit will come.

The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. — Galatians 5:22.

We'd love to manufacture patience on a morning when we're running low, produce peace on demand, generate love by sheer willpower. But notice the word Paul uses: the “fruit” of the Spirit. Not the “production” of the Spirit, nor the “manufacturing.” Fruit isn't made in a factory; it grows on a living tree, slowly, from the inside.

This distinction changes everything. Fruit is the natural result of a healthy life, not of relentless effort. No one has ever seen an apple tree strain to produce an apple. It draws from its roots, receives the sap, and the fruit appears in its season. In the same way, love, joy, and peace aren't performances to be forced out, but the overflow of a life connected to the Spirit.

That doesn't mean you have nothing to do: you have to abide, to stay connected to the source. Your role isn't to manufacture the fruit, but to tend the conditions for its growth. Where the Spirit is free to work, in a heart that abides in Christ, fruit always appears in the end — even if it's slower than we'd like.

For you today: what fruit are you trying to manufacture by willpower alone — patience, gentleness, peace? Stop forcing it. Come back to the source instead. Spend time with the Spirit, let Him flow through you. What you can't produce by effort, He will grow by His life.

A transformed character isn't decreed in a day; it grows, season after season, in a life that abides in Christ. Be patient with the process, as a gardener is with a tree. The fruit of the Spirit isn't manufactured: it grows, surely, when you abide.

Be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is. — Romans 12:2.

We can reduce life in the Spirit to a matter of usefulness: being employed by God, serving, producing, accomplishing things for Him. And that is a real part of it. But if we stop there, we miss a deeper desire of God's heart. The Spirit doesn't just want to use you like a tool; He wants to transform you like a son.

The difference is immense. A tool is used without being changed; it stays what it is and is put to work for a task. A son is loved for who he is, and his full flourishing is desired. God could accomplish His work by any means. If He involves you in what He is doing, it isn't first for what you produce, but for what He wants to make of you along the way.

This guards us against a common trap: seeking power without pursuing likeness. We can crave gifts, effectiveness, and impact while neglecting our own hearts. But the Spirit isn't content simply to channel His strength through you; He wants to renew your mind, reshape your desires, and make you like Christ. Being used without being transformed would be a fool's bargain.

For you today: are you mostly seeking to be useful to God, or are you also giving Him the right to transform you? Open to Him not only your hands to serve Him, but your heart to be changed. Ask Him not only, “Use me,” but, “Transform me.”

God used Jonah, despite himself, to save Nineveh; but the story doesn't end there. The book closes on the prophet's hard heart, which God is still seeking to transform. Usefulness wasn't enough; God also wanted to change him. Don't settle for being an instrument in His hands: let Him make you a new person.

You will know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes from thornbushes or figs from thistles? — Matthew 7:16.

There is something dazzling about gifts. A talent, eloquence, success, a visible anointing impress people, draw them in, get them talking. And it's easy to confuse the impression a gift makes with the depth of a life. But Jesus shifts our gaze: He doesn't say “you will know them by their gifts,” but “by their fruits.” Gifts impress; fruit reveals who you really are.

The difference is crucial. A gift can operate independently of character: you can preach beautifully about love and live in harshness, exercise a powerful ministry and hide a heart in ruins. Fruit doesn't cheat. Love, patience, humility, and faithfulness in everyday life tell the truth about a life far better than any display of talent.

This invites us not to be dazzled—not by others, and not by ourselves. It's tempting to feel reassured about your spiritual life by looking at your gifts, your results, what shines. But the real question isn't “What can I do?” It's “What fruit is my life producing, over time, where no one is applauding?”

For you today: Do you measure your life by what impresses or by the fruit you truly bear? Don't neglect your gifts, but don't stop there. Ask God to grow in you the fruit that reveals a transformed heart: practical love, gentleness, integrity.

Judas had all the outward gifts of a disciple: he preached, he cast out demons, he was one of the Twelve. But in the end, the fruit revealed what the gifts had hidden. Don't let yourself be defined by what shines: let your life be known by its fruit, because it's the fruit, not the gift, that reveals who you are.

titre: Christlikeness, the Proof of the Spirit
texte:
But we all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as by the Spirit of the Lord. — 2 Corinthians 3:18.

We often imagine that the mark of the Spirit is power: dazzling manifestations, spectacular gifts, a strength that impresses. And God does act with power, that's true. But Paul shows us a deeper and surer sign: the Spirit transforms us “into the same image,” the image of the Lord. The real proof of His presence isn't the extraordinary things you do, but who you are slowly coming to resemble.

Look at the movement of the verse: we behold the glory of the Lord, and by beholding Him, we become like Him. We aren't transformed by staring at ourselves or by flexing our spiritual muscles. We change by looking at Jesus. What you behold shapes you. The Spirit doesn't fix your eyes on your performance; He turns your face toward Christ until His features become yours.

“From glory to glory”: the resemblance is progressive. It doesn't come all at once, in a single experience. It is woven day after day, in a thousand details where your character begins to look like His: more patience where you used to explode, more gentleness where you used to cut people off, more love where you used to judge. It's slow, but it's real. And that, far more than the high moments, is what proves the Spirit is at work.

This truth frees you from exhausting comparison. You don't have to chase after other people's power or judge yourself by what you produce. The question isn't “Am I as powerful as they are?” but “Do I look a little more like Jesus than I did yesterday?” The Spirit isn't trying to make you a star; He is working to make you a living portrait of Christ.

So don't measure your spiritual life by the intensity of your experiences, but by the resemblance that is growing. Offer Him your unveiled face, without a mask, and let Him transform you as you behold Him. Power fades; likeness to Jesus remains. And that is the surest sign that the Spirit lives in you.

titre: My House Will Serve the Lord
texte:
But as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. — Joshua 24:15.

Every family serves something. No one ever says it out loud, but it shows: in what fills the evenings, in what makes voices rise, in what gets celebrated and what goes unspoken. Some homes serve success, others comfort, others peace at any cost, even at the cost of truth. A home without a choice is never neutral: it simply ends up serving whatever shouts the loudest.

At the end of his life, Joshua sets a decision before the people: “Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve.” Then he gives his own answer, without waiting for anyone else to follow: “As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.” He doesn't say “once everyone agrees,” or “when the kids are older.” He makes a decision as the head of his household, in the present tense.

It's hard, because a home is built in everyday life, not in grand speeches. We'd love to have children who love God, a marriage that prays, a home at peace, but we keep putting off praying together, sharing the Word at the table, asking forgiveness before bed. Yet what isn't chosen every day eventually stops being chosen at all.

For you today: what small step can you take so that God has a real place under your roof? A two-minute prayer before a meal, a verse read at night, a blessing spoken over your children, a “I'm sorry” you dare to say first. You don't need a perfect family to begin; you need a decision. And if you live alone, your home matters too: what you allow into your home shapes who you become.

Joshua didn't wait for everyone to agree before committing. He spoke for himself and for his own, and his choice marked an entire generation: Israel served the Lord all the days of Joshua. One faithful decision can change the atmosphere of an entire home. So choose today. Your home won't become holy by chance; it will become holy because someone decided it would.

God sets the lonely in families. — Psalm 68:6.

Loneliness isn't always visible. You can be surrounded at work, smile in photos, tell everyone “I'm fine,” and come home at night to a heavy silence. There is the loneliness of those who live alone, of elderly people no one calls anymore, of young people who can't find their place anywhere, and, crueler still, of those who feel alone among their own.

The psalmist makes a magnificent declaration about God's heart: “God sets the lonely in families.” He doesn't just comfort the lonely from a distance. He settles them somewhere. God is a Father who gathers, and the Church was born of that desire: a family you enter not by blood, but by grace.

But family isn't something you live from afar. Many wait for others to come to them, and end up concluding that no one cares about them. Yes, God gives a family, but He also calls us to step into it, to open the door, to let others know us. Healing from loneliness often comes through a step we dread.

For you today: if you feel alone, tell God plainly, then take a step toward His family. Join a home group, stay after the service, accept the invitation you would have turned down. And if you are well surrounded, look at who is alone around you: the widow on the third floor, the young person who always sits in the back, the coworker no one invites. You may be the family God wants to give them.

At the foot of the cross, Jesus saw His mother and the disciple He loved. He said to Mary, “Woman, behold your son,” and to the disciple, “Behold your mother.” From that hour, the disciple took her into his own home. At the very moment He was giving His life, Jesus was creating a new family. No one is an orphan in God's house.

For a righteous man may fall seven times and rise again. — Proverbs 24:16.

We often dream of a Christian life without falls. We imagine that true believers move forward in a straight line, with no missteps, no relapses, no going backward. So when we fall again, into the same sin, into the same discouragement, we tell ourselves: “I'm not cut out for this. Others make it, but not me.”

Yet the proverb says something very realistic: “A righteous man may fall seven times and rise again.” The righteous fall. Not once by accident: seven times, meaning as many times as it takes. What makes someone righteous isn't the absence of falls, it's the fact that they get back up. The difference between the one who moves forward and the one who gives up isn't decided in the fall, but in what comes next.

The enemy loves to turn a fall into an identity. He whispers: “You fell, so you're a failure. Stay down.” But God doesn't see you that way. He doesn't count your falls to crush you; He reaches out His hand to set you back on your feet. His grace doesn't run out at the seventh time.

For you today: where have you fallen recently? Don't stay on the ground despising yourself. Acknowledge your wrong before God, plainly and without excuses, and receive His forgiveness. Then get up and take the next right step. If a fall keeps coming back, dare to talk about it with someone you trust: what is brought into the light loses much of its power.

Peter denied Jesus three times, the very night he had promised to die for Him. He could have stayed in his shame. But he came back, and a few weeks later he was preaching before thousands of people on the day of Pentecost. The righteous person isn't the one who never falls. It's the one who always gets back up.

Be strong and of good courage; do not be afraid, nor be dismayed, for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go. — Joshua 1:9.

There are moments when you have to move forward while everything in you wants to pull back. A new job, a move, a diagnosis, a difficult conversation, a call from God that feels far beyond you. Your legs shake, your heart races, and a little voice keeps saying, “You're not good enough.” We wait to feel less afraid before we move. But fear doesn't always leave.

Joshua was in that very place. Moses, the great leader, had just died. And now it was up to him to lead an entire people into a land full of enemies. In a single chapter, God tells him three times, “Be strong and of good courage.” Why repeat it so often, unless Joshua was afraid? God doesn't scold him for his fear. He gives him a reason to move forward in spite of it: “the Lord your God is with you wherever you go.”

Biblical courage isn't a matter of temperament. It isn't reserved for people who are afraid of nothing. It's a decision grounded in a presence. You can tremble and obey at the same time. Courage means not letting fear have the last word, because Someone else has already spoken.

For you today: what are you afraid to step into? Name it. Then take this verse as both a command and a promise: “Be strong and of good courage, for the Lord your God is with you.” Take a step, even a small one, even while trembling. You don't need to see the whole road; you need to know who is walking with you.

A few days later, Joshua and the people found themselves facing the Jordan at flood stage. The priests had to set their feet in the water before the river parted. The miracle followed the step of faith. Courage isn't the absence of fear. It's moving forward because God is with you.

titre: Your Gifts in Service to Others
texte:
As each one has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. — 1 Peter 4:10.

Many Christians think they don't really have a gift. They look at those who preach, sing, or lead, and they tell themselves, “I don't have anything special.” So they stay on the sidelines, convinced that others will do better than they could. And all the while, gifts God has placed in them stay wrapped, never opened.

Peter is very clear: “As each one has received a gift, use it to serve one another.” Each one. No one is left out. He speaks of the “manifold grace of God,” like a palette of a thousand colors. There's the gift of speaking, but also of welcoming, encouraging, organizing, comforting, giving, fixing, praying. None is small when it's put to use in service.

Peter also uses an important word: stewards. A steward isn't an owner; he manages what belongs to someone else. Your gifts aren't yours for your own glory. They've been entrusted to you for the good of others. The danger isn't only hiding your gift, but also using it to put yourself forward. A gift is fully revealed when it serves.

For you today: what do people often come to ask you for? What do you do with joy that brings good to those around you? That may well be your gift. Ask God to show you where to put it to use. Then take a concrete step: offer your help to your church, to a neighbor, to someone in need. Gifts grow when you use them.

Dorcas, in Joppa, was neither a preacher nor a prophetess. She made tunics and garments for widows. When she died, all those women came weeping to show Peter what she had sewn for them. Her quiet gift had touched an entire town. Your gift wasn't made to shine. It was made to serve.

If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. You are the body of Christ. — 1 Corinthians 12:26-27.

In a church, it's easy to feel useless. You see the people on the platform, the ones who speak, the ones who organize, and you tell yourself you don't bring much to the table. Or, on the flip side, you feel indispensable and look down on those who seem less committed. Either way, you forget who we really are.

Paul uses a powerful image: “You are the body of Christ, and members individually.” In a body, every member has a function. The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you.” And the members that seem weaker are, Paul says, necessary. No one is extra. No one is above the others.

And a body lives together. When you stub your toe, your whole body feels it. Paul says, “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all rejoice with it.” That is how the Church should work: weeping with those who weep, rejoicing with those who rejoice, without jealousy and without indifference.

For you today: do you feel useless, or, on the contrary, above others? Take your place in the body again, no higher and no lower. Then look around you: who is suffering in your community and needs you to suffer alongside them? Who is experiencing a joy you can sincerely share? A message, a visit, a prayer, a word of congratulations: that is how the body holds together.

When Saul was persecuting the Church, Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus and said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?” He didn't say “My disciples”; He said “Me.” Whatever touches a member touches the Head. You are part of Christ. In His body, no one is extra, and no one is alone.

titre: The Temple of the Holy Spirit
texte:
Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? — 1 Corinthians 6:19-20.

Our generation has a strange relationship with the body. On one hand, we idolize it: we show it off, sculpt it, compare it. On the other, we mistreat it: excess, lack of sleep, addictions, self-contempt. Caught between worshiping the body and neglecting it, many no longer know how to see it. And even among Christians, some think the body has nothing to do with the spiritual life.

Paul declares something astonishing: “Your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit.” In the Old Testament, the temple was the place where God dwelt among His people. Now, your body is that place. God doesn't live only in your soul; He dwells in all of you. Your body isn't some unimportant shell; it is a sacred dwelling.

Paul adds: “You are not your own, for you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God in your body.” This isn't a prison; it's a dignity. Caring for your body, keeping it pure, respecting it, and respecting the bodies of others is a way of worshiping. What you do with your body says something about the One who lives in it.

For you today: how do you treat your body? Do you neglect it, overexpose it, despise it? Choose one concrete step to honor it: sleep better, eat better, get moving, give up an excess, guard your purity. And if you struggle to love your body, remember that God chose to dwell in it. What He inhabits, He does not despise.

When Jesus entered the temple in Jerusalem and found it full of merchants, He overturned the tables and said, “My house shall be called a house of prayer.” He took seriously the holiness of the place where God dwelt. Your body is that place today. It isn't an object to display or to despise. It is a temple to honor.

Nevertheless I have this against you, that you have left your first love. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent and do the first works. — Revelation 2:4-5.

Do you remember the early days of your faith? That hunger to read the Bible, that joy in prayer, that urge to tell everyone about Jesus, those tears during worship. Then the years went by. You grew stronger, more committed, more experienced. But something may have quietly cooled. You still do the things, but the fire isn't the same.

Jesus sends a message to the church in Ephesus. He begins by commending it: it works hard, it perseveres, it rejects false teachers, it hasn't grown weary. A model of an active, faithful church. Then He adds: “Nevertheless I have this against you, that you have left your first love.” All that activity couldn't make up for what mattered most. They were serving Jesus, but they no longer loved Him the way they did at first.

This is a real danger for those who have been serving for a long time. Service can replace relationship. Habits can become a heartless routine. We know the songs, the verses, the answers, but we've lost the wonder. And Jesus isn't satisfied with our works; He wants our heart.

For you today: is your love for Jesus as alive as it was at the beginning? Jesus gives three steps: remember, repent, and do the first works. Remember what used to set your heart on fire. Acknowledge before Him what has grown cold. Then go back to what you did at the beginning: time alone with Him, His Word read with hunger, worship from the depths of your heart.

In the Song of Songs, the beloved hears her lover knocking at her door in the night. She hesitates, makes excuses, delays opening. When she finally gets up, he is gone, and she searches for him throughout the city. Don't let habit make you miss His visit. You can do everything for Jesus and forget to love Him.

Even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you. See, I have engraved you on the palms of My hands. — Isaiah 49:15-16.

“God has forgotten me.” It's a thought many people don't dare say out loud, but they feel it. When prayers go unanswered, when trials pile up one after another, when others seem blessed and we don't, we wonder if God has lost sight of us. As if we had fallen off His list, tucked away somewhere in a corner of His memory.

The people of Israel, in exile, were saying exactly that: “The Lord has forsaken me, and my Lord has forgotten me.” And God answers with the tenderest image there is: “Can a woman forget her nursing child?” It's almost unthinkable. Then He adds: “Even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you.” God's love goes beyond even the strongest human love.

And He gives proof: “See, I have engraved you on the palms of My hands.” Sometimes we write an important name on our hand so we won't forget it. But God didn't write it in ink; He engraved it. And reading this, how can we not think of the hands of Jesus, pierced by the nails? Your name is inscribed there forever, at the price of His blood.

For you today: in what area do you feel forgotten by God? Tell Him honestly, just as Israel did. Then listen to His answer. He hasn't forgotten you. He can't forget you. Look at the cross: it is the engraved proof that you are in His heart. And even if you don't yet understand what He is doing, you can be sure He hasn't let go of you.

After His resurrection, Jesus appeared to Thomas and said to him: “Reach your finger here, and look at My hands.” The marks were still there. Even in His glorified body, He keeps the scars of His love for us. You may feel forgotten by everyone. But your name is engraved on God's hands.

Zacchaeus, make haste and come down, for today I must stay at your house. — Luke 19:5.

Some people think they are too far gone for God. Their reputation is bad, their past is heavy, they've made choices they regret. They tell themselves they first need to change, make amends, become a good person, before they can draw near to Jesus. So they keep their distance, curious perhaps, but convinced they are not welcome.

Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, and he was rich. In other words, he collaborated with the Roman occupiers and grew wealthy at the expense of his own people. Everyone despised him. Being short, he climbed a sycamore tree to catch a glimpse of Jesus in the crowd. He wanted to see without being seen. But Jesus stopped under the tree, looked up, and called him by name.

Jesus didn't say, “Change first, and then I'll come.” He said, “Today I must stay at your house.” He invited Himself into the home of the man everyone avoided. The crowd grumbled. But it was this unconditional welcome that transformed Zacchaeus. He didn't change in order to be accepted; he changed because he had been accepted.

For you today: is there an area of your life where you think you're too far gone for Jesus? Hear Him calling you by name. He isn't asking you to make yourself presentable before you come. He wants to come into your home, today, just as you are. Open the door to Him. And look around you: who are the “Zacchaeuses” the people around you despise, whom Jesus wants to reach through you?

Zacchaeus hurried down and received Him joyfully. Then he stood up and said, “Look, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold.” Jesus replied, “The Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost.” Jesus isn't waiting for you at the top of the ladder. He invites Himself in right where you are.

A threefold cord is not quickly broken. — Ecclesiastes 4:12.

Some couples love each other sincerely and yet wear down. The years go by, weariness sets in, misunderstandings pile up, and what was once a passion becomes a fragile routine. Then you wonder how a love so strong at the start could grow so thin. Often, it isn't love that's missing. It's the strength to carry it.

Ecclesiastes observes a simple truth: two are better at getting back up, keeping warm, standing firm. Then it adds an image: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” Two braided strands already hold. But a third strand changes everything. In a marriage, that third strand is God Himself. He isn't a decoration on the wedding day; He is what holds the other two together when they weaken.

The trap is counting only on the other person to hold things together. We expect our spouse to fill every gap, never to disappoint, always to be patient. No human being can carry that weight. When each of you draws from God first, you come to the other no longer to demand, but to give. And the marriage can breathe.

For you today: what place does God truly hold in your marriage, or in the one you hope to build? Invite Him in, in practical ways. Pray together, even awkwardly, even in two sentences. Bless each other out loud. Hand your conflicts over to Him instead of letting them fester. If you're single, start braiding that strand now: the most beautiful gift you can give your future spouse is a life already bound to God.

Aquila and Priscilla are almost always mentioned together in the New Testament. They worked side by side, opened their home to the Church, and served God hand in hand. Their strength didn't come only from getting along, but from their shared calling. When God is at the center, love no longer rests on two fragile strands. It becomes a cord that storms cannot easily break.

When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take me in. — Psalm 27:10.

Rejection leaves marks that time doesn't always erase. A parent who walked away, a spouse who left home, friends who turned their backs, a community that let you down at the worst possible moment. And deep in your heart, a question lingers: “What's wrong with me that people leave?”

David writes a sentence of heartbreaking honesty: “My father and my mother forsake me.” He doesn't downplay the pain. He dares to name the deepest wound there is. But he doesn't stop there: “then the Lord will take me in.” The word evokes someone being picked up, gathered, brought into a home. Where others left you by the side of the road, God bends down to take you in.

Rejection lies to us about our worth. It makes us believe we're unwanted, that we don't deserve to be loved, that the next person will end up leaving too. So we protect ourselves, we grow suspicious, we no longer dare to get attached. But your story isn't defined by those who let go of you. It's defined by the One who never lets go.

For you today: what rejection is still speaking louder than God's love in your life? Name it before Him, as David did. Then listen to what God says about you: you are chosen, you are wanted, you are welcomed. And if the wound is too raw to carry alone, don't be ashamed to ask a brother, a sister, or a pastor for help.

Jesus Himself knew rejection. He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. His disciples abandoned Him when He was arrested. He knows what you feel. But He said: “The one who comes to Me I will by no means cast out.” Those who let go of you don't have the last word. God takes you in.

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me?” — John 21:17.

Some failures feel like ones we'll never recover from. We've let God down, let others down, let ourselves down. We no longer feel worthy to serve, worthy to be used, barely worthy to be forgiven. So we step back, convinced the page has turned and our calling died with our fall.

By the lake, after the resurrection, Jesus prepares a charcoal fire and a meal for His disciples. It was around a charcoal fire that Peter had denied Him three times. And it is around a charcoal fire that Jesus asks him the same question three times: “Do you love Me?” He doesn't ask him to explain his failure. He doesn't put him on trial. He goes straight to the heart.

Three denials, three questions, three declarations of love. Jesus doesn't reopen the wound to humiliate Peter; He heals it point by point. And with each answer, He entrusts him with a mission: “Feed My sheep.” The man who had failed becomes the shepherd of the flock. Jesus' restoration doesn't just put you back on your feet; it sends you back on mission.

For you today: what failure made you believe your calling was over? Draw near to Jesus. Let Him ask you the question that truly matters: “Do you love Me?” Answer Him honestly, even if your love seems small. Then listen to what He entrusts to you. He isn't finished using you.

Peter was grieved that Jesus asked him a third time. But he answered, “Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You.” He no longer leaned on his own promises, but on the gaze of Jesus. That is where solid faith is born. Jesus isn't asking if you've failed. He's asking if you love Him.

Though it tarries, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry. — Habakkuk 2:3.

You prayed. You believed. You waited. And nothing seems to move. The door stays shut, the healing is slow in coming, the person you carry in prayer hasn't changed, the dream you gave to God is still sitting in a drawer. And a small voice starts to whisper: “If He isn't answering, maybe He said no.”

But waiting is not God's silence. Habakkuk had received a promise for later, and God told him: “Though it tarries, wait for it; because it will surely come.” What God has promised already has its date; it just isn't written in your calendar. A delay from God is not a denial from God. Between the promise and its fulfillment, He hasn't gone anywhere: He is preparing the ground, shaping hearts, and very often, He is preparing you.

It's hard, because we live in an age of instant everything. Everything is delivered in twenty-four hours, everything downloads in a few seconds, and we end up expecting the same from God. But God is not a vending machine; He is a Father. And a father doesn't just give what is good: he gives it at the right time. What comes too soon can damage the very thing it was meant to bless.

For you today: what promise have you finally put away because it was taking too long? Take it back out. Lay it before God again, not with impatience, but with trust. And while you wait, don't stand still: obey what He is showing you today, serve where you are, keep your heart tender. Waiting is not wasted time; it is the time when God forms in you what the answer alone could never form.

Abraham waited twenty-five years for the promised child. Joseph spent thirteen years between the pit and the prison before he saw his dreams fulfilled. Neither of them was forgotten: God was right on time, His time. So hold on. What is delayed is not canceled. The promise is on its way, and the One who made it does not lie.

For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many. — Mark 10:45.

In the world, greatness is easy to spot: the higher you climb, the more people serve you. Places of honor, titles, privileges, influence. Even in the Church, the temptation is there to seek recognition, visibility, first place. We want to serve God, but we also like it when people notice.

Jesus' disciples were no different. James and John had just asked Him for the two best seats in His kingdom, and the others were indignant, probably because they wanted the same ones. Jesus gathers them together and turns everything upside down: “Whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” Then He gives His own example: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.”

The Son of God had every right to be served. He chose to serve. He washed feet, touched lepers, fed crowds, made time for children, and ultimately gave His life. Service isn't a step on the way to greatness; in the kingdom of God, it is greatness itself.

For you today: where are you waiting to be served rather than serving? At home, at work, at church? Today, choose an act of service no one will notice: put away what others left behind, help without being asked, listen to someone who needs it. Do it without saying a word. What you do in secret, your Father who sees in secret sees.

At the Last Supper, not one disciple got up to wash the others' feet; that was a servant's job. So Jesus, the Master, took the towel and the basin. He showed us the way. The greatest is not the one who is served. It's the one who serves.

Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ. — Galatians 6:2.

Everyone is carrying something. Behind the Sunday smiles, there are money worries, children who cause concern, marriages that are wavering, illnesses, grief, secret battles. But often, no one says a word. Out of modesty, out of pride, out of fear of being judged, or because we don't want to be a bother. So each person carries it alone, believing everyone else is doing fine.

Paul tells the Galatians: “Bear one another's burdens.” The word describes a heavy load, too heavy for one person. God never intended for us to carry everything alone. He gave us a family, so we could take turns, support one another, and share the weight. And Paul says this is how we fulfill the law of Christ, the law of love.

Carrying other people's burdens requires seeing them. You have to slow down, ask real questions, listen without judging, and stay when things get hard. And so that others can carry our burdens, we have to be willing to show them. The humility to ask for help is just as important as the generosity to offer it.

For you today: what burden have you been carrying alone for too long? Dare to share it with someone you trust. And look around you: who seems to be carrying a load that's too heavy? Offer practical help, not just words: a meal, babysitting, a ride, a time of prayer together. Love shows up in shoulders that are offered.

When Jesus was walking toward Golgotha, exhausted, the soldiers compelled a man, Simon of Cyrene, to carry His cross behind Him. Even the Son of God accepted help to carry His burden. A shared burden isn't necessarily lighter, but it is no longer carried alone.

We demolish arguments and every lofty thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive to obey Christ. — 2 Corinthians 10:5.

The most important battlefield of your life is between your ears. Thoughts show up without warning: fear, accusation, doubt, jealousy, impurity, discouragement. It feels like you have no control over them. They loop over and over, at night, when you wake up, and they end up becoming certainties.

Paul uses military language: “We demolish arguments” and “we take every thought captive to obey Christ.” He isn't describing a passive attitude. Thoughts aren't guests we just have to put up with. We can stop them, question them, hold them up to God's truth, and refuse the ones that set themselves up against Him.

A thought isn't a sin just because it crosses your mind. But what we do with it matters. We can welcome a thought, feed it, and chew on it until it becomes a stronghold. Or we can take it captive: “Is this true? Is this what God says?” If it isn't, we replace it with the truth.

For you today: what thought keeps coming back and pulling you away from peace? “I'm worthless,” “God has forgotten me,” “this will never change”? Write it down. Then look up what the Word says about it, and write that truth right next to it. Every time the thought comes back, answer it with that truth, out loud if you need to. A captive thought loses its power.

Paul writes to the Philippians: “Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.” He doesn't just ask us to drive out bad thoughts, but to feed the good ones. You can't stop a thought from passing through. But you can stop it from settling in.

By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to the place which he would receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. — Hebrews 11:8.

We like to see what's ahead. Before we commit, we want to know the details: where, when, how, for how long, with what guarantees. And when God calls us to something new without giving us all the answers, we hesitate. We wait until we have the whole map before taking the first step.

Abraham received a radical call: leave his country, his family, his father's house, and go to a land God would show him. He was seventy-five years old. No map, no detailed plan, no arrival date. Just a promise and a voice. And the text simply says: he obeyed and went out, not knowing where he was going.

That is faith. Not a complete absence of questions, but a trust stronger than the questions. Abraham didn't know where he was going, but he knew who he was going with. His security didn't come from the destination, but from the One who was calling. And that walk into the unknown made him the father of all who believe.

For you today: is there a call from God you haven't answered because you couldn't see the whole road? A change, a ministry, a decision, a step of faith? Ask God for clarity for the next step only. Then take it. You don't need to know everything to obey. You need to trust the One who does.

The wise men left the East following a star. They didn't know exactly where it would lead them or what they would find. But they kept moving forward, step by step, until they bowed down before the child Jesus. Faith doesn't always know the destination. It knows the One who calls.

The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty one who saves; He will make you His greatest joy. — Zephaniah 3:17.

Many believers picture God as a stern judge watching them with a frown. They think He tolerates them, puts up with them, waits for them to do better. So they live out their faith in fear and guilt, never daring to believe that God could take pleasure in them.

The prophet Zephaniah paints a stunning picture: “The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty one who saves; He will make you His greatest joy.” And the verse goes on: “He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing.” God doesn't merely save you; He delights in you, He sings for joy over you.

It's not because you are perfect. This passage is addressed to a people who had failed badly. But God, after cleansing and forgiving them, turns toward them with overflowing joy. It is the love of a father who sees his child coming home, of a husband gazing at his beloved. In Christ, you are God's joy, not because of your performance, but because of His grace.

For you today: how do you picture God looking at you? Frowning, or smiling with joy? Take a few minutes to meditate on this verse. Picture God rejoicing over you with songs of joy. Let this truth heal your fear and your guilt. You can draw near to Him with confidence, like a beloved child.

In the parable, when the prodigal son comes home, the father doesn't wait with his arms crossed. He sees him from far off, he runs, he throws his arms around his neck, he kisses him, and he throws a party. He rejoices far more than he reproaches. That is God's heart for you. He doesn't put up with you. He delights in you.

Then he said to Jesus, “Remember me when You come into Your kingdom.” And Jesus said to him, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” — Luke 23:42-43.

We sometimes think it takes a long life of faithfulness to deserve heaven. Years of service, prayer, and good works. And those who have wasted their lives, who reach the end of the road with a heavy past, supposedly don't really stand a chance anymore. It would be too late for them. Too late to change, too late to be saved.

On Golgotha, three crosses. In the center, Jesus. On either side, two criminals. One mocks Jesus along with the crowd. But the other rebukes him: “We are receiving what we deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong.” Then he turns to Jesus and simply says, “Remember me when You come into Your kingdom.” No grand theology, no good works to show. Just a look of faith toward Jesus.

And Jesus' answer is immediate: “Today you will be with Me in Paradise.” Not in a few years, not after a period of trial. Today. This man was never baptized, never took Communion, never served in a church. He simply acknowledged his wrong and put his trust in Jesus. That is the whole grace of the Gospel.

For you today: do you think it's too late for you, or for someone you love? As long as there is breath, there is hope. Turn your eyes to Jesus, right now. And keep praying for those who seem far away. A single look of faith is enough for Jesus to answer. He hasn't changed since that cross.

Jesus told the story of workers hired at different hours to work in a vineyard. Those who came at the last hour received the same wage as those hired in the morning. Some thought it was unfair. But that's how grace works: it isn't a wage, it's a gift. It is never too late to turn your eyes to Jesus.

Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it. — Proverbs 22:6.

We all want to pass the faith on to our children. So we talk, we explain, we correct, we repeat. And sometimes it feels like nothing is sinking in. Yet children take in far more than we think. It's just that they don't first remember what we say. They remember what we live.

“Train up a child in the way he should go,” says the proverb. The Hebrew word carries the idea of initiating, dedicating, setting someone on their way. We don't train only with lessons, but with a path we walk ahead of them. A child learns prayer by seeing their parents pray, forgiveness by seeing their parents forgive each other, trust by seeing how they go through hard times.

That's demanding, because it confronts us with our own consistency. A child quickly senses the difference between a faith recited on Sunday and a faith lived out on Tuesday night. They don't need perfect parents; they need real parents, who admit their wrongs, who ask for forgiveness, who come back to God when they fall. That is what makes faith believable in their eyes.

For you today: what do your children, or the young people around you, see of your relationship with God? Let them catch you praying. Tell them about a prayer God answered. Bless them at night. If you've failed in front of them, dare to tell them you're sorry: it may be the most beautiful Gospel lesson you ever give them.

Timothy had received the faith from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, even before he met Paul. These two women are known for only one thing: a sincere faith, passed on at home. And Paul reminds him that from childhood Timothy had known the Holy Scriptures. What is sown patiently in a child's heart is never lost. Your words matter, but your life speaks louder.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted! — Matthew 5:4.

Some losses cut life in two: a before and an after. The passing of a parent, a child, a spouse, a friend. We discover that grief is not a straight line. It comes back in waves, triggered by a song, a scent, a date. And sometimes we no longer even dare to talk about it, as if sadness should have an expiration date.

Jesus says something surprising: “Blessed are those who mourn.” He doesn't say that pain is good, or that you have to smile no matter what. He says that those who weep are not forgotten: “they shall be comforted.” The blessing He speaks of is not the absence of tears; it is the presence of a Comforter in the midst of them.

Many Christians think that having faith means not crying. But the Bible is full of tears: Abraham weeps for Sarah, David weeps for his son, Jesus weeps for His friend. Faith doesn't erase sorrow; it keeps it from turning into despair. We grieve, but not like those who have no hope.

For you today: is there a loss you are carrying in silence? Give yourself permission to talk to God about it, even with clumsy words, even with cries. Let Him into your sadness instead of holding it at a distance. And if someone around you is grieving, don't search for the perfect words. Be there. A faithful presence often comforts better than any speech.

In Nain, Jesus came upon a funeral procession: a widow was following her only son to the grave. The text says He had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” Then He gave the young man back his life. That day, He showed what He will one day do for all who are His. God doesn't ask you to hide your tears. He promises to comfort them.

titre: Though I Fall, I Will Rise
texte:
For when I fall, I will arise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord will be a light to me. — Micah 7:8.

There are moments when it feels like everyone is waiting for you to fall. Judging looks, hurtful comments, people who almost seem glad to see you on the ground. And sometimes the harshest voice is your own: “See? You'll never make it.” The darkness seems to have won.

The prophet Micah speaks on behalf of a people who have fallen, and he addresses the enemy who mocks: “Do not rejoice over me! For when I fall, I will arise.” He doesn't deny the fall. He doesn't pretend everything is fine. But he refuses to let the fall have the last word. And he adds: “when I sit in darkness, the Lord will be a light to me.”

Notice: this isn't pride talking. Right after, the prophet admits: “I will bear the indignation of the Lord, because I have sinned against Him.” Biblical hope is not arrogance. It is the humble certainty that God lifts up those who return to Him. The one who acknowledges his wrong can also proclaim his restoration.

For you today: is there someone, or an inner voice, rejoicing over your fall? Answer it with this word. Say it out loud: “Though I fall, I will rise.” Then turn toward the light: confess what needs to be confessed, receive forgiveness, and trust God with what comes next. Tonight's darkness is not your final chapter.

Jonah was swallowed by a great fish, the consequence of his own running away. From the depths of that night, he prayed, and God brought him back to dry land and entrusted him with his mission once again. He had fallen very low; God set him back on his feet. Your fall is not your finish. It is the very place from which God will lift you up.

If it is possible, as much as depends on you, live peaceably with all men. — Romans 12:18.

There are people with whom peace seems impossible. A neighbor who's always looking for a fight, a coworker who criticizes everything, a family member who keeps stirring up old quarrels. You've tried, you've made the effort, and nothing changes. So you end up telling yourself, “With him, it's just not possible.”

Paul is surprisingly realistic: “If it is possible, as much as depends on you, live peaceably with all men.” He acknowledges that peace doesn't always depend on us. You can't force another person's heart. But he sets a clear standard: the part that depends on you, do it fully. Never let the obstacle to peace come from your side.

That changes the question. Instead of asking, “Why is he like that?” you ask, “What depends on me?” Maybe a gentler tone, a reply you hold back, a grudge you let go, a step toward the other person, a prayer for them. Peace often begins with what you refuse to add to the conflict.

For you today: with whom is peace difficult? Take an honest inventory of your part: your words, your reactions, your silences. Choose one gesture that depends on you: a greeting, an apology, an act of service, a kind prayer for that person. Then entrust to God what doesn't depend on you. You're not responsible for the other person's response, only for your share of peace.

Abraham and Lot had flocks that were too large, and their herdsmen were quarreling. Abraham, the elder, could have imposed his choice. Instead he said to Lot, “Please let there be no strife between you and me.” And he let him choose the best portion. God blessed Abraham far beyond what he had given up. You can't force peace. But you can refuse to be the war.

He who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much. — Luke 16:10.

We often dream of great things for God. A ministry that reaches thousands of people, an important work, a visible impact. And while we dream, we neglect the little things: being on time, keeping our word, simple tasks, faithfulness in the details. We tell ourselves that's not where what really matters happens.

Jesus says the opposite: “He who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much.” The little things are not a side detail; they are the training ground. That's where character, integrity, and perseverance are formed. Whoever cheats on a small amount will cheat on a large one. Whoever keeps their word in small commitments will keep it in big ones.

God sees what people don't notice. Service done when no one is watching, honesty when no one is checking, consistency when no one is applauding. These small acts of faithfulness don't make noise, but they build a solid life. And it's often to those who were faithful in the shadows that God entrusts more.

For you today: what little thing have you neglected, telling yourself it wasn't important? A promise you made, a service you started, a daily prayer, a bill, a word owed to someone? Pick it back up. Do it well, with care, for God. Faithfulness isn't proven in the big moments; it's built in the ordinary ones.

David faithfully kept his father's sheep, defending the flock against the lion and the bear, when no one saw him. It was that hidden faithfulness that prepared him to face Goliath, and then to shepherd God's people. God will not entrust you with great things as long as you despise the little ones.

But exhort one another daily, while it is called “Today,” lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. — Hebrews 3:13.

We underestimate the power of an encouraging word. A simple message: “I prayed for you this morning.” A comment: “You did well.” A sincere question: “How are you really holding up?” These words cost almost nothing, and yet they can lift up someone who was about to give up. But we often keep them to ourselves, thinking others don't need them.

The author of Hebrews tells us to exhort one another “daily.” Not once in a while, not just at church. Every day. Why such urgency? “Lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.” The heart hardens slowly, silently. And encouragement among believers is one of the ways God keeps hearts tender.

Exhorting isn't lecturing. It's calling someone to your side, strengthening them, reminding them of God's truth when they forget it. Sometimes gently, sometimes firmly, always with love. And the phrase “while it is called ‘Today’” reminds us that time is limited. Tomorrow's encouragement may come too late.

For you today: who is God putting on your heart to send a word of encouragement to? Don't put it off. Write that message now. Share a verse that touched you, tell that person what you appreciate about them, remind them that God hasn't forgotten them. And if you need encouragement yourself, dare to tell a brother or sister.

Barnabas's real name was Joseph. The apostles nicknamed him Barnabas, which means “son of encouragement.” He was the one who welcomed Paul when everyone else was suspicious of him, and who encouraged the church in Antioch. His influence changed history. A word of encouragement today can prevent a fall tomorrow.

titre: Don't Lean on Your Own Understanding
texte:
Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He shall make your paths straight. — Proverbs 3:5-6.

We like to understand before we act. Weigh the pros and cons, analyze, anticipate. That's often wise. But there are moments when our understanding reaches its limits. A situation that makes no sense, a direction that seems illogical, a trial we can't explain. And we get stuck, because we refuse to move forward without understanding everything.

The proverb gives a three-part instruction. First: “Trust in the Lord with all your heart.” Not halfway, not with a backup plan. Next: “lean not on your own understanding.” It doesn't say not to think, but not to make your thinking your foundation. Finally: “in all your ways acknowledge Him.” In big decisions and small ones alike, invite Him in.

And the promise follows: “He shall make your paths straight.” He doesn't promise you'll understand everything. He promises to make the path passable. Often, understanding comes after obedience, not before. We understand when we look back at how God led us, while moving forward we could only see one step at a time.

For you today: what decision or situation are you trying to solve with your own intelligence alone? Bring it to God, in detail. Ask Him for His direction. Listen to His Word, the counsel of wise people, the peace or unrest in your heart. Then take the step He shows you, even if you can't yet see the whole road.

Naaman, a Syrian general with leprosy, was told to dip himself seven times in the Jordan. It seemed absurd to him; the rivers of Damascus looked better. At first he was angry. But when he obeyed, his flesh became like that of a little child. Your understanding is limited. Your trust in God doesn't have to be.

I heard the voice of the Lord, saying: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am! Send me.” — Isaiah 6:8.

When people talk about mission, service, or calling, many of us step back. “I'm not qualified. I've never studied the Bible. I'm not a good speaker. I have too many flaws.” We look at what we don't have, and we wait for God to call someone else, someone more skilled, more holy, more ready.

Isaiah had an extraordinary vision of God's holiness. And his first reaction was to feel undone: “Woe is me, for I am undone! Because I am a man of unclean lips.” He didn't feel worthy at all. But a seraph touched his lips with a burning coal and said to him, “Your iniquity is taken away.” Only after he had been cleansed did he hear God's question.

And God's question wasn't, “Who is the most qualified?” but, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” God was looking for someone available. Isaiah answered before he even knew what the mission was: “Here I am! Send me.” His availability came before the details. It is God who qualifies those He calls.

For you today: what is keeping you from saying “here I am” to God? Your past, your limitations, your fears? First let Him cleanse you and reassure you. Then simply tell Him, “Here I am, send me.” Start right where you are: in your family, your workplace, your church, your neighborhood. God always has something to entrust to an available heart.

When Jesus called His first disciples, He didn't go looking for the teachers of the law. He called fishermen by the lake. They left their nets and followed Him. Their only qualification was their availability. God isn't looking for capable people. He's looking for available people.

“For My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways My ways,” says the Lord. — Isaiah 55:8-9.

There are things God does, or allows, that we don't understand. A prayer answered for someone else but not for us. A trial that strikes the most faithful person. A door that closes just when everything seemed to line up. And we want explanations. We want God to account to us, for everything to fit together according to our logic.

God answers through Isaiah: “My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways My ways.” Then He gives an image: “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher than your ways.” The distance between His understanding and ours is as great as the distance between heaven and earth. We see a fragment; He sees the whole picture.

This isn't a way to silence us. It's an invitation to humility and trust. A child doesn't always understand why his father says no, or why he has to wait. But if he knows his father's love, he can trust him even without understanding. Trust begins where understanding ends.

For you today: what situation don't you understand? You have the right to bring your questions to God. But also choose to trust Him. Tell Him: “I don't understand, but I know who You are. You are good, You are wise, You are faithful.” Hold on to His character when His ways seem dark to you.

Job lost everything without understanding why. He cried out, questioned, protested. When God finally spoke to him, He didn't give him an explanation, but He revealed Himself to him in His greatness. And Job said: “I have heard of You by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees You.” When you don't understand His ways, trust His heart.

For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life. — John 3:16.

It may be the best-known verse in the Bible. You see it on signs in stadiums, you learn it as a child, you quote it so often that you eventually stop hearing it. It has become familiar, almost commonplace. And yet every word of this verse holds an ocean of love that a whole lifetime isn't enough to explore.

“For God so loved.” This isn't a lukewarm, conditional, measured love. It is a love beyond measure. “The world.” Not just the good, the religious, those who deserve it, but the whole world, with all its rebellion and all its wounds. “That He gave His only begotten Son.” God's love didn't stop at words; He gave what was most precious to Him.

“That whoever believes in Him.” Whoever. No one is left out of the invitation. There are no conditions of background, past, or merit. Only believing, that is, trusting Jesus. “Should not perish but have everlasting life.” God doesn't want to lose us; He wants us to live. A life that begins now and will never end.

For you today: read this verse again slowly, as if for the first time. Replace “the world” with your own name: “God so loved [your name] that He gave His only begotten Son.” Let this truth touch you. Then think of someone around you who doesn't know this love. How could you show it to them, or tell them about it, this week?

Abraham was commanded to offer his only son, Isaac. At the last moment, God stopped his hand and provided a ram in his place. What God spared Abraham, He did not spare Himself. He gave His own Son. God's love isn't measured by what He says, but by what He gave.

“Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise, “that it may go well with you and that you may live long on the earth.” — Ephesians 6:2-3.

For some, this commandment is a joy: their parents were a shelter, a school of love, an example. For others, it's a thorn. There were absences, harsh words, injustices, sometimes deep wounds. And when we read “Honor your father and mother,” something tightens inside: how can I honor what hurt me?

In the Bible, to honor doesn't mean approving of everything or pretending nothing happened. The word speaks of weight, of value: recognizing that these people hold a unique place in your story, because God used them to give you life. You can set healthy boundaries, refuse what is wrong, and still choose not to despise. Paul points out that this is the first commandment with a promise: God attaches a blessing to it.

Contempt is a quiet poison. It settles into sighs, mockery, icy silences, and in the end it damages the one who carries it even more than the one who receives it. To honor is sometimes to give thanks for what was good, even if it was little. It's praying for them. It's speaking to them with respect, even when you disagree. And as they grow older, it's taking care of them.

For you today: what is your attitude toward your parents, in your words and in your thoughts? If they're still here, take a step: a call, a thank-you, a visit, a word that honors them. If there's a wound, bring it to God first, and ask Him for the grace to forgive without denying what happened. If they're no longer here, honor their memory by holding on to the best of what they passed on to you.

On the cross, in the midst of His own suffering, Jesus thought of His mother. He entrusted Mary to the disciple He loved, so she wouldn't be left alone. Even in agony, the Son of God honored the one who had carried Him. If He did it in that moment, we can, by His grace, learn to honor in turn. To honor doesn't mean approving of everything. It means never despising.

titre: The Inner Man Is Being Renewed
texte:
Even though our outward man is perishing, yet the inward man is being renewed day by day. — 2 Corinthians 4:16.

There are days when the body reminds you of its limits. The illness that settles in, the pain that won't go away, the fatigue that a night's sleep no longer fixes, the years that pass and leave their mark. You look at what you can no longer do, and a kind of sadness sets in: “I'm not who I used to be.”

Paul knew this. He had been beaten, stoned, worn out by his travels, scarred by trials. And yet he writes: “We do not lose heart.” He doesn't deny reality: his outward man is perishing. But he discovers another, deeper reality: his inward man is being renewed day by day. There is a life in you that illness cannot reach and that the years cannot age.

Our culture worships youth and performance. It measures a person's worth by what they produce. So when the body weakens, we feel useless. But God doesn't see the way the world sees. A bedridden person who prays can bear more fruit than a restless crowd. The vigor of the soul doesn't depend on the strength of the body.

For you today: if your body is causing you pain, don't let that weakness define your worth. Every morning, offer the day to God and ask Him to renew your heart. Pray for others from your bed, encourage someone with a message, bless someone with a word. And if you're in good health, take care of those who no longer are: a visit can renew far more than just a day.

Caleb was eighty-five years old when he said, “I am still as strong as I was on the day Moses sent me. Give me this mountain!” His body had aged, but his faith had stayed young. What is renewed in God doesn't get wrinkles. Your body may wear out. Your soul can grow younger every day in Him.

Forgetting those things which are behind and reaching forward to those things which are ahead, I press toward the goal. — Philippians 3:13-14.

The past has a strange power. It comes back as regret: “If only I had…” It comes back as nostalgia: “Things were better back then.” It comes back as wounds that replay the same scene over and over. And if you keep looking back long enough, you end up not moving forward at all. You live in the present, but your mind stayed in yesterday.

Paul had a heavy past: he had persecuted the Church and had Christians arrested. He also had a glorious past: a flawless religious record, a reputation, titles. And he says: I forget what lies behind. Neither his failures nor his successes were to hold him back. He reached toward what was ahead, like a runner straining toward the finish line.

Forgetting, here, doesn't mean erasing it from memory. Paul remembered his past very well. It means refusing to let it run what comes next. You can't change yesterday, but you can stop handing it the keys to tomorrow. God's forgiveness has dealt with your failures, and His promises are greater than your past victories.

For you today: what is still pulling you backward? A regret, an old wound, a past glory you miss? Name it before God. Hand it over to Him once and for all. Then ask yourself just one question: what is the next step God is expecting from me? Take that step. We rarely move forward in one leap; we move forward one step at a time, eyes fixed ahead.

Lot's wife turned around to look at what she was leaving behind, and she was frozen in place. Jesus said: “Remember Lot's wife.” A gaze turned backward paralyzes. A gaze turned toward Christ makes you run. You can't run forward while constantly looking behind you.

I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content. I know how to be abased, and I know how to abound. — Philippians 4:11-12.

We often tell ourselves, “I'll be happy when…” When I get that job, that house, that salary, that spouse, that child. And when we get there, the satisfaction lasts a few weeks, then a new longing takes its place. The finish line keeps moving back. We chase a happiness that's always one step ahead.

Paul writes these words from a prison. He has neither comfort nor freedom. And he says, “I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content.” The key word is “learned.” Contentment isn't a personality trait reserved for a few. It's something you learn. Paul had known hunger and abundance, and he discovered that his peace depended on neither one.
