But our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also eagerly wait for the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ. — Philippians 3:20.

We are attached to our country, our culture, our roots. That's natural, and it's good. But it's easy to let our identity shrink down to just that: our nationality, our background, our political or social affiliation. And sometimes these affiliations take up so much room that they divide us, even among Christians.

Paul is writing to the Philippians. Philippi was a Roman colony, and its people were proud of their Roman citizenship, with all its privileges. Paul reminds them of a higher citizenship: “our citizenship is in heaven.” They lived in Philippi, but they truly belonged somewhere else. They were ambassadors of another kingdom.

Being a citizen of heaven doesn't mean despising the earth. It means living here according to the values of another kingdom. Loving your enemies, serving instead of dominating, forgiving, sharing. It also means putting what divides us into perspective. A Christian from Africa, Europe, Asia, or the Americas shares the same citizenship. What unites us in Christ is stronger than what separates us.

For you today: what defines your identity the most? Your country, your culture, your party, your success? Remember that your first citizenship is heavenly. Live today as an ambassador of that kingdom: at work, in your family, in your neighborhood. And look at your brothers and sisters from other backgrounds as fellow citizens.

An ancient letter described the early Christians as people who live in their own homeland, but as foreigners passing through. They took part in everything as citizens, while knowing that their true homeland was elsewhere. That is our calling. You live on earth, but your passport comes from heaven.

titre: Loving as Christ Loved the Church
texte:
Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself for her. — Ephesians 5:25.

Marriage is often lived as a contract of exchange: I give if you give, I do my part if you do yours. And as soon as the scales tip, we feel cheated. We keep score, we compare, we demand. Little by little, the home becomes a courtroom where each one argues for their rights.

Paul completely overturns that logic. He asks husbands to love their wives “just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself for her.” The model isn't a love that waits for what it's owed, but a love that gives first. Christ didn't love the Church because she was perfect; He gave Himself for her in order to make her beautiful. His authority comes through the cross, never through coercion.

This verse is addressed to husbands, but it sheds light on the whole couple: in the same passage, Paul calls each one to submit to the other in the fear of Christ. Biblical love doesn't first look for what it can receive, but for what it can offer. It listens before answering, serves before being served, protects instead of crushing, forgives instead of keeping score.

For you today: if you're married, ask yourself in what area you expect from your spouse what you no longer give yourself. Choose one concrete act of giving: listening without your phone, a service no one notices, a word of encouragement, a sincere apology. If you're not married, look at what model of love you're preparing in your heart: the one that demands, or the one that gives itself.

On the evening of His last meal, Jesus rose from the table, took a towel, and washed His disciples' feet, Peter included, Judas included. The Master became a servant, and then He told them, “I have given you an example.” The Christian couple begins right there, on its knees, towel in hand. Loving like Christ isn't demanding to be served. It's choosing to give yourself.

Instead of your shame you shall have double honor. — Isaiah 61:7.

Shame is different from guilt. Guilt says, “I did something wrong.” Shame says, “I am something wrong.” It clings to you. Sometimes it comes from our own mistakes, sometimes from what others have made us endure. And it pushes us to hide, to lower our eyes, to believe we are unworthy of being loved.

Through the prophet Isaiah, God makes an astonishing promise to a humiliated people: “Instead of your shame you shall have double honor.” He doesn’t just promise to erase the shame. He promises to replace it with an even greater honor. This chapter opens with the words Jesus read in the synagogue in Nazareth, before declaring, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled.”

Shame lies to us about our identity. It makes us believe that our worst moment says who we are. But in Christ, it isn’t your past that defines you; it’s the way He sees you. He doesn’t just forgive you from a distance: He lifts you up, so you can walk with your head held high again.

For you today: what shame still makes you lower your eyes? A past sin, abuse you suffered, a public failure, a tarnished reputation. Bring it to Jesus. He won’t look at you with disgust. Listen to what He says about you: forgiven, washed, loved, honored. And refuse to let shame have the last word on what you believe about yourself.

The woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years was excluded, considered unclean. She touched Jesus’ garment in secret, hoping to slip away afterward. But Jesus looked around for her, brought her forward in front of everyone, and called her “daughter.” He healed her body and restored her honor. Where shame has covered you, God wants to cover you with honor.

Death and life are in the power of the tongue. — Proverbs 18:21.

We speak without thinking. Thousands of words every day, at home, at work, on social media. A sarcastic remark, a hurtful nickname, a passing criticism, one more complaint. We tell ourselves, “They’re just words.” But some words heard twenty years ago still echo in people’s hearts. And others, spoken at the right moment, have saved lives.

The proverb leaves no room for neutrality: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” Your mouth has the power to build up or tear down, to lift up or crush, to bless or to curse. James compares the tongue to a small spark that can set a whole forest ablaze. This small member has an outsized influence.

This power also works on yourself. What you tell yourself all day long shapes what you believe. “I’m worthless,” “I’ll never make it,” “nobody loves me”: words like these, repeated over and over, become prisons. On the other hand, declaring what God says about you feeds your faith and opens up new paths.

For you today: listen to your words. The ones you speak to others, and the ones you speak to yourself. Do they bring life? Choose today to speak at least one word that builds up: sincere encouragement, gratitude, a blessing. And if you’ve hurt someone with your words, don’t wait to make it right.

God created the world by His word: “Let there be light!” And we, made in His image, have received a share of that power: our words also create atmospheres, relationships, destinies. Jesus said we will give an account for every idle word. Your words build up or tear down. They are never neutral.

titre: Free from the Love of Money
texte:
Let your conduct be without covetousness; be content with such things as you have. For He Himself has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” — Hebrews 13:5.

Money is not a taboo subject in the Bible. Jesus talks about it very often, because He knows how deeply it touches the heart. You can have little and be obsessed with money, just as you can have a lot and remain free. The problem isn't first in your wallet, but in the place money takes in your thoughts, your fears, and your choices.

The author of Hebrews connects two things we don't often link together: the love of money and the fear of being abandoned. “Be content with such things as you have. For He Himself has said, ‘I will never leave you.’” Deep down, we cling to money because it gives us an illusion of security. We think that with enough, we'll be safe. But no amount can protect us from everything.

True security doesn't come from what we possess, but from the One who possesses us. When God promises He will never abandon us, He touches the root of our fear. If He is there, lack no longer has the power to crush us, and abundance no longer has the power to seduce us. Then we can manage money instead of being managed by it.

For you today: what place does money take in your thoughts? Is it a source of constant worry, or of envy? Entrust your finances to God in prayer, in concrete ways. Thank Him for what you have. And take a step of freedom: give, even a little, with joy. Generosity is the best proof that money is not your master.

A rich man once came to ask Jesus how to inherit eternal life. Jesus looked at him, loved him, and invited him to give everything away and follow Him. The man went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. He owned a lot, but it was his possessions that owned him. You don't need to have everything when you have the One who never leaves you.

Let us consider one another in order to stir up love and good works, not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together. — Hebrews 10:24-25.

It has become easy to live out your faith alone. You listen to sermons online, you pray at home, you read your Bible in your own corner. And when the Church has let you down, or relationships there get complicated, you tell yourself: “I can follow God just fine without other people.” Little by little, you drift away, and the flame dies down without you even noticing.

The author of Hebrews was writing to Christians who were weary, persecuted, and tempted to give up. And he told them: “Let us not forsake the assembling of ourselves together, as is the manner of some.” Even back then, some were getting into the habit of no longer showing up. But he reminds us why we need one another: to watch over one another, to encourage each other to love and to do good.

The Church is not a show you watch; it's a family you belong to. It isn't perfect, because it's made up of people like you and me. But that's where God has chosen to make us grow: through the friction of relationships, through mutual forgiveness, through serving side by side. No one becomes a mature disciple alone.

For you today: what place does the Church hold in your life? If you've drifted away, honestly ask yourself why, and dare to come back. If you're there, don't settle for just attending: connect. Join a small group, greet someone new, check in on someone who's been missing. Be the one who watches over others.

There's a story about a pastor who visited a man who had stopped coming to church. Without a word, he took an ember from the fire and set it apart. Within minutes, it went out. Then he placed it back among the others, and it glowed again. The man understood. A lone ember eventually goes out. Together, they keep the fire burning.

The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light. — Matthew 6:22.

Our eyes are being pulled at like never before. Thousands of images scroll past our fingertips every day. Ads, videos, shows, social media. We think what we watch doesn't really affect us, that it's just entertainment. But every image leaves a mark, and what we look at long enough ends up shaping what we desire.

Jesus says: “The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light.” The eye is a doorway. What comes in through it either lights up or darkens everything inside. Jesus says this right after speaking about treasures: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. What you look at reveals what you desire, and feeds what you love.

This isn't only about impurity. An eye can also grow dark through envy, by constantly looking at what others have. Through fear, by binging on bad news. Through comparison, by gazing at idealized lives. Keeping your eye healthy means carefully choosing what you let in.

For you today: what do you actually look at the most? Check your screen time, and be honest. Does it light up your heart or darken it? Do some sorting: unfollow what drags you down, limit what pulls you away from God. And give your eyes something beautiful to gaze at: the Word, creation, the faces of those you love.

One evening, from the roof of his palace, David saw a woman bathing. He looked, then he sent someone to find out about her, then he had her brought to him. One lingering look led to adultery, and then to murder. It all started with the eye. What you gaze at long enough ends up living in your heart.

Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth! — Psalm 46:10.

We live in constant motion. We rush from one task to the next, notifications interrupt us nonstop, and even our moments of rest are filled with noise. When problems come, we respond by doing even more: more effort, more strategies, more control. And the idea of stopping seems almost irresponsible.

Psalm 46 describes a world in total chaos: the earth giving way, the mountains shaking, the nations raging, the kingdoms tottering. And in the middle of that turmoil, God says: “Be still, and know that I am God.” The word carries the idea of letting go, laying down your weapons, ceasing to strive. It isn't inaction; it's trust.

To be still is to acknowledge that we are not God. That the world doesn't rest on our shoulders. That our efforts, as necessary as they may be, are not what holds the universe together. It is in that stillness that we “know” He is God. Not just in our heads, but in our hearts. Restlessness blocks that knowing; stillness makes it possible.

For you today: in what situation are you striving instead of trusting? Take five minutes, right now, to stop. Turn off your phone. Breathe. Slowly repeat this verse: “Be still, and know that I am God.” Hand over to Him whatever is stirring you up. Then go back to your day knowing that you are not the one exalted over the earth, He is.

Martha was busy and distracted preparing a meal worthy of Jesus. Mary, her sister, had sat down at His feet to listen to Him. Martha complained, and Jesus answered her: “Martha, Martha, you are worried and troubled about many things. But one thing is needed.” Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is stop.

For with God nothing will be impossible. — Luke 1:37.

There are situations where you've run all the numbers, and the conclusion is final: it's impossible. The doctors have run out of options. The money won't be enough. That person will never change. The door is shut for good. And eventually you stop praying, because you can't see how God could possibly step in.

The angel Gabriel comes to tell Mary that she will give birth to the Son of God. She is a virgin. Humanly speaking, it's impossible. So the angel gives her a sign: her relative Elizabeth, old and barren, is six months pregnant. Then he adds these words that have echoed through the centuries: “For with God nothing will be impossible.”

This verse is not a magic formula for getting everything you want. It is a revelation of who God is. What is impossible for us poses no difficulty for Him. He is not limited by the laws of nature, by circumstances, or by human decisions. And He acts according to His wisdom and His love.

For you today: what situation have you filed under “impossible”? Dare to bring it back before God. Pray again, with faith. And like Mary, answer with trust: “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” Surrender the situation and your will to Him. He is able to do far more than you can imagine.

Abraham and Sarah had laughed at the idea of having a child in their old age. God then asked, “Is anything too hard for the Lord?” A year later, Isaac was born. What is impossible for you is never too hard for God.

Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst. But the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life. — John 4:14.

We are all thirsty for something. Thirsty for love, for recognition, for meaning, for peace, for joy. And we try to quench that thirst however we can. In a relationship, a success, a purchase, a pleasure, a distraction. It works for a while. Then the thirst comes back, often stronger. We drink again, and we are thirsty again.

Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, in the middle of the day. She comes to draw water, as she does every day. And Jesus speaks to her about another kind of water: “Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst.” This woman had had five husbands and was living with a sixth man. She had tried to quench her thirst, without ever succeeding.

Jesus doesn't lecture her about morality. He offers her what her heart was truly seeking. And He makes it clear that this water will become a spring within her. Not a bottle you have to keep refilling, but an inner spring that wells up. It is the Spirit of God who comes to dwell in us and fills what nothing else can fill.

For you today: which wells are you drawing from to quench your thirst? What always leaves you unsatisfied? Be honest. Then come to Jesus and ask Him for living water. Take time in His presence, in His Word, in prayer. Let Him fill what the other wells can never fill.

The Samaritan woman left her water jar by the well and ran into the town, saying, “Come, see a Man who told me all things that I ever did.” She had come looking for water; she left with a spring. What can't fill your heart will always end up leaving you thirsty.

titre: Unto Us a Child Is Born
texte:
For unto us a Child is born, unto us a Son is given; and the government will be upon His shoulder. And His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. — Isaiah 9:6.

At Christmas, we talk a lot about gifts, meals, decorations, and family reunions. These are beautiful things. But the heart of Christmas can easily get lost under the wrapping paper. We celebrate a birth without really stopping to consider the One who was born. And yet, this birth changed the history of the world.

More than seven hundred years before Jesus was born, the prophet Isaiah announced it: “Unto us a Child is born, unto us a Son is given.” Notice the two verbs: a Child is born, that is His humanity; a Son is given, that is God’s gift. And this Child bears extraordinary names: Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. A baby in a manger, and at the same time God Himself.

God could have come in power and glory, surrounded by armies. He chose to come small, fragile, in a stable, born to humble parents. No one is afraid to approach a baby. The shepherds came, and so did the wise men, the poor as well as the learned. God made Himself approachable. He took on our condition to meet us right where we are.

For you today: which name of Jesus do you need to hear? Wonderful, if you have lost your sense of wonder. Counselor, if you no longer know what to do. Mighty God, if you are facing the impossible. Everlasting Father, if you feel alone. Prince of Peace, if your heart is troubled. Choose that name, and pray to Jesus, calling Him by it.

That night, shepherds were keeping watch over their flocks in the fields. Simple people, often looked down upon. It was to them that the angel appeared first, announcing great joy: “For there is born to you a Savior.” They went with haste and found the Child. God did not come as a conqueror. He came as a child, so that no one would be afraid to draw near.

A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. — Proverbs 15:1.

A curt remark, a rising tone, a message that stings. In a split second, everything in you gears up to strike back. The words come on their own, sharper than the other person's. We call it “answering.” In reality, it's often pouring fuel on the fire, then being surprised that the house burns down.

The proverb is disarmingly simple: “A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” Gentleness is not weakness. It takes far more strength to hold back a hurtful word than to let it fly. The gentle person isn't someone without an opinion; it's someone who stays in control of their mouth when everything pushes them to lash out.

We don't always choose the conflicts that come our way. But we do choose what we add to them. Every answer is a crossroads: either it escalates the tension, or it opens a path to peace. A gentle word doesn't deny the problem; it makes it possible to talk about it without tearing each other apart.

For you today: in which relationship do conversations turn sour the fastest? At home, at work, on social media? Practice one simple thing: before you answer, breathe, and silently ask the Spirit to put gentleness on your lips. Lower your voice instead of raising it. Write your message, then wait before sending it. You'll be amazed how many storms die down when you stop blowing on them.

When Gideon returned from victory, the men of Ephraim sharply rebuked him because he hadn't called them. He could have defended himself and humiliated them. Instead, he chose to honor them: “What have I done now in comparison with you?” And the text says that their anger toward him subsided. You don't always choose the storm. But you do choose whether you add wind to it.

It is enough! Now, Lord, take my life […] Then, behold, an angel touched him and said to him, “Arise and eat.” — 1 Kings 19:4-5.

There is a kind of exhaustion that a night's sleep can't fix. You've given everything, you've held on for a long time, and one day, something gives way. You don't want anything anymore, you have no strength left to pray, no desire left to fight. You feel empty, useless, and a dark thought settles in: “It is enough. I can't go on.”

Elijah had just experienced one of the greatest victories of his life on Mount Carmel. Then a single threat from Jezebel was enough to make him collapse. He fled into the wilderness, sat down under a broom tree, and asked to die. The great prophet was worn out, discouraged, at the end of his rope. The Bible doesn't hide this moment. It tells it, so that we would know that even men of God can hit rock bottom.

What is so moving is God's response. He doesn't scold him. He doesn't demand more faith from him. He sends an angel who touches him and says, “Arise and eat.” Bread, water, sleep, and then more bread. God cares for the exhausted body before speaking to the wounded heart. He knows what we are made of.

For you today: if you're at the end of your rope, don't condemn yourself. Tell God the truth: “I can't go on.” Then accept His simple care: rest, a meal, a walk, a word from a friend, an appointment with someone who can help you. Taking care of yourself is not a lack of faith. And if thoughts of death overwhelm you, talk to someone you trust or to a professional right away.

After that time of rest, Elijah walked to the mountain of God, where he heard the still, small voice. God gave him a new mission and a companion, Elisha. His story didn't end under the broom tree. Neither will yours. When you can't go on, God doesn't start with a sermon. He starts by lifting you up.

titre: Each Day Has Enough Trouble of Its Own
texte:
Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will take care of itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble. — Matthew 6:34.

Worry loves the future. It dreams up scenarios, expects the worst, replays conversations that haven't even happened yet. What if this happens? What if that doesn't work out? What if I get sick, lose my job, or my kids drift away? We live today under the weight of tomorrow, and even the day after. The present day gets crushed beneath troubles that don't exist yet.

Jesus says: “Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will take care of itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.” He doesn't say tomorrow will be easy. He acknowledges that every day has its share of difficulties. But He asks us to carry only today's share. God doesn't give tomorrow's grace today; He will give it tomorrow.

It's like the manna in the wilderness: every morning, the Israelites gathered the portion for that day. Those who tried to save some for the next day found it spoiled. God wanted to teach His people to depend on Him day by day. Worry is trying to gather tomorrow's manna with today's strength.

For you today: what worry about the future is filling your mind? Write it down, then deliberately hand it over to God. Then ask yourself: what depends on me today? Do it, simply. The rest belongs to tomorrow, and tomorrow belongs to God. When worry comes back, bring your mind back to the present, where God gives you His strength.

In the same passage, Jesus teaches us to look at the birds of the air and the lilies of the field. They don't worry, and yet the Father feeds them and clothes them. How much more will He take care of you. God gives you today's grace. Don't waste it carrying tomorrow.

And whatever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord and not to men. — Colossians 3:23.

Many people treat their work as a break from their spiritual life. On Sunday, we worship God. Monday through Friday, we earn a living. The office, the job site, the cash register, the classroom, the house with the kids: so many places where God seems absent. And we wait for the weekend to find a little meaning again.

Paul wrote these words to slaves. People who hadn't chosen their work, which was often grueling and sometimes unjust. And he told them: “Whatever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord.” He didn't promise them their situation would change right away. He offered them a new way to live out their work: no longer for a human master, but for Christ Himself.

That changes everything. A repetitive task, done for the Lord, becomes an offering. Work done well, even when no one sees it, becomes a testimony. Honesty in little things, patience with a difficult coworker, care given to a detail: all of it becomes worship. There is no longer any separation between the sacred and the everyday.

For you today: what work do you do reluctantly? Before you start, take a moment to offer it to God: “Lord, I'm doing this for You.” Do it with care, even if no one thanks you. Be a person of integrity, even when you could cut corners. And be a presence of peace in your workplace. That's often where people will see Jesus in you.

Joseph, a slave in Potiphar's house and later a prisoner, always worked with excellence. The text says the Lord made all he did prosper. Even in a place he hadn't chosen, he served God. And it was that faithful work that prepared him for the palace. Your work becomes worship when you do it for Him.

Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! — Psalm 133:1.

Divisions have been part of the Church's story from the very beginning. Disagreements over details, personality clashes, jealousy, unresolved hurts. We split apart, we criticize each other, we grow suspicious. And the watching world sees Christians who talk about love but can't get along.

David sings of a reality that is far too rare: “How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” Unity is not uniformity. Brothers aren't necessarily alike; they have different personalities, opinions, and stories. But they choose to stay together. Unity is a choice made again and again, not the absence of differences.

The psalm ends with a promise: “For there the Lord commanded the blessing—life forevermore.” There. In unity. God has tied His blessing to the way we live together. Jesus prayed that His disciples would be one, so that the world would believe. Our unity isn't a luxury; it's a testimony.

For you today: are you a builder of unity or of division? In your family, your church, your circle of friends? Refuse to take part in criticism and gossip. Look for what brings people together rather than what pulls them apart. Pray for those you struggle with. And if a relationship is damaged, take a step toward reconciliation. Unity is built one small choice at a time.

On the day of Pentecost, the disciples were all together in one place. They had prayed with one accord for days. It was on this united community that the Spirit came down, and the Church was born. Where brothers choose unity, God chooses to bless.

Catch us the foxes, the little foxes that spoil the vines, for our vines are in blossom. — Song of Solomon 2:15.

Big falls make a lot of noise. But most spiritual lives don't collapse all at once. They wear down slowly, through little things we let slide. One skipped prayer, then two, then ten. A small lie we think doesn't matter. A cutting remark in our marriage. A compromise we allow ourselves “just this once.” Nothing serious, on the surface.

In the Song of Solomon, the picture is striking: “Catch us the foxes, the little foxes that spoil the vines.” It isn't lions threatening the vineyard, but little foxes. They slip in quietly, nibble the young shoots, and damage the blossoms. And the text adds: “for our vines are in blossom.” It's precisely when something beautiful is coming to life that the little foxes are most dangerous.

This verse speaks of love, and it applies especially to relationships. Couples rarely die from one big crisis, but from an accumulation of small neglects: less listening, less tenderness, more irritation. The same is true of our relationship with God. What we tolerate in small things eventually damages what was in bloom.

For you today: what little foxes are prowling in your vineyard? In your life with God, in your marriage, in your family, in your integrity? Name them. Then catch them while they're still small: pick back up the habit you lost, repair the careless word, correct the small compromise. What gets dealt with early prevents great damage.

Samson didn't lose his strength all at once. He played with danger, again and again, thinking he was untouchable. Each small concession seemed harmless, until the day he woke up without his strength, not knowing that the Lord had departed from him. It isn't always the great storms that destroy. Often, it's the little foxes.

And Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him. — Genesis 5:24.

Genesis chapter 5 is a long list of names. So-and-so lived so many years, fathered sons and daughters, and then he died. So-and-so lived so many years, and then he died. A litany that reminds us how brief life is. And suddenly, in the middle of that list, one man stands out. Of Enoch, it is not first said that he died, but that he walked with God.

We know almost nothing about Enoch. No great feat, no great battle, no spectacular achievement. Only this, repeated twice: he walked with God. For three hundred years, day after day, he journeyed with Him. To walk with someone is to go at the same pace, in the same direction, in conversation. It's not a sprint; it's a relationship that lasts.

The author of Hebrews says that Enoch had this testimony: that he pleased God. What pleased God wasn't first his performance, but his faithful presence. You can do a lot for God without walking with Him. And you can walk with Him in a life that looks ordinary, making each day a shared step.

For you today: are you running for God, or are you walking with Him? Slow down. Invite Him into your day, not just at the start, but all the way through: on your commute, in your decisions, in your conversations. Talk to Him like a traveling companion. A walk isn't done all at once; it's built step by step, every day.

Enoch's story ends in a unique way: “he was not, for God took him.” A Jewish tradition pictures it like this: God and Enoch walked so far together that one day God said to him, “We're closer to My home than to yours. Come.” God isn't looking for people who run for Him, but for people who walk with Him.

Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine! — Isaiah 43:1.

In an increasingly anonymous world, it's easy to feel like just a number. A file number, a user ID, one subscriber among thousands. We fill out forms, we wait our turn, we blend into the crowd. And sometimes we wonder whether anyone truly knows us, beyond what we show.

God speaks to His people in exile, discouraged and forgotten. And He doesn't speak to them as an anonymous crowd. He says: “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine!” In the Bible, knowing someone's name means knowing their deepest identity. God doesn't just know that you exist; He knows you, personally.

And He adds: “you are Mine.” This isn't cold ownership; it's a loving belonging. Like a parent who says of their child, “That one's mine.” You have been redeemed; you are precious in His eyes. Right after, He says: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.” The One who knows your name walks with you through your trials.

For you today: do you feel lost in the crowd, forgotten, unimportant? Listen to God calling you by name. Take a moment to read this verse with your own name in it: “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name, [your name]; you are Mine!” Let this truth reach you. You matter to Him.

On the morning of the resurrection, Mary Magdalene was weeping before the empty tomb. She saw Jesus without recognizing Him, thinking He was the gardener. Then He spoke a single word: “Mary!” And everything changed. She recognized Him by the way He said her name. You are not a number to God. He knows your name.

Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with Me. — Revelation 3:20.

This verse has often been used to invite unbelievers to accept Jesus. But who is Jesus actually speaking to? The church in Laodicea, a Christian church. A rich, comfortable, self-assured church that thought it needed nothing. And Jesus was outside, knocking at the door of His own Church.

It's a striking picture. You can be a Christian, go to church, know the Bible, and still have left Jesus outside your everyday life. We invite Him on Sunday, but we close the door on Monday. We give Him a place in some rooms of our house, but not in all of them. And He patiently keeps knocking.

Jesus doesn't force the door. He respects our freedom. But He knocks, He calls, He waits. And His promise is intimate: “I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with Me.” In biblical culture, sharing a meal meant sharing your life. Jesus doesn't just want to be invited; He wants to sit at the table with you, in a close, everyday relationship.

For you today: is there a door in your life that you've closed to Jesus? Your work, your finances, your leisure, your marriage, your thoughts? Listen: He is knocking. Open that room to Him. Invite Him into the places you haven't yet let Him enter. And take time to “dine” with Him: a real moment of fellowship, without rushing.

On the road to Emmaus, two discouraged disciples walked with Jesus without recognizing Him. When they reached their home, they urged Him: “Stay with us.” He came in, sat at the table with them, and as He broke the bread, their eyes were opened. Jesus never forces the door of your heart. He knocks, and He waits for you to open.

Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here; for He is risen, as He said. — Matthew 28:5-6.

Friday had been the darkest day in history. Jesus, the one in whom His disciples had placed all their hope, had died on a cross. On Saturday, everything was silent. The disciples were hiding, devastated, convinced it was all over. And on Sunday morning, a few women went to the tomb, not to find life, but to anoint a dead body.

But the tomb was empty. The stone had been rolled away. And an angel said to them: “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here; for He is risen, as He said.” As He said. Jesus had foretold His death and His resurrection. What looked like defeat was part of His victory.

The resurrection is not a minor detail of the Christian faith; it is its very foundation. Paul says that if Christ is not risen, our faith is futile. But He is risen. That means sin has been defeated, death has lost its power, and life has the last word. What is true for Jesus will be true for all who belong to Him.

For you today: is there an area of your life that feels like a hopeless Friday or a silent Saturday? A dead relationship, a buried dream, a situation that seems over? Remember: Sunday is coming. The God who raised Jesus can make life spring up where you see only death. Bring Him what seems buried.

The women left the tomb with fear and great joy. On the way, Jesus Himself came to meet them and said, “Rejoice!” They came, took hold of His feet, and worshiped Him. He was alive. He still is. The empty tomb is proof that death does not have the last word.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 1
texte:
Day 1. I Have the Right to Not Be Okay.

There are days when everything feels heavier. You lack energy, courage, desire. And when you're a Christian, guilt can sometimes add to the discomfort: "I should be okay. I should be joyful. I should have more faith."

But Christians aren't superheroes. Faith doesn't make us immune to fatigue, sadness, fear, or discouragement. The Bible doesn't hide the moments of weakness of those who loved God. Elijah found himself so exhausted he wanted to die. David wept and wondered why his soul was cast down. Paul knew distress and dejection.

Not being okay doesn't mean I'm a bad Christian. It doesn't mean God has abandoned me either. I can simply recognize what's happening in me without condemning myself.

Maybe today, the first thing God expects of me isn't to be strong, but to be real. I can stop pretending. I can say: "Lord, today, I'm not doing well."

Jesus doesn't call to him those who have everything under control. He calls those who are weary and burdened. I don't need to get better before I come to him. I can come as I am, with my fatigue, my questions, and my tears.

Today, I allow myself to not be okay. And in the midst of my weakness, I choose to draw near to God rather than hide from him.

Remember — I don't need to be okay to come to God.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 2
texte:
Day 2. I Can Tell God Everything.

When we pray, we can be tempted to present to God an "acceptable" version of what we feel. We choose the right words, we try to have the right attitude, and we sometimes hide emotions we're ashamed of.

Yet God is our Father. And a child should be able to speak to his father with truth.

I can tell God I'm sad. I can tell him I'm afraid, disappointed, frustrated, or exhausted. I can even tell him I'm angry, even when that anger is directed at him. God already knows my heart. Hiding what I feel from him doesn't protect him and doesn't heal me.

The Psalms are full of surprisingly honest prayers. David asks God how long he will forget him. He expresses his anguish, his questions, his fear, then lets God gradually transform his perspective.

Verbalizing an emotion before God doesn't mean that emotion is always right. It simply means I give him access to what's actually happening in me. I can lay before him an unfair thought, excessive anger, or irrational fear and allow him to comfort me, correct me, and lead me toward the truth.

I don't need to impress God with my prayer. I can speak to him like a Father who loves me.

So today, I can take a few minutes and tell him exactly what's on my heart. Without filter. Without mask. Without trying to be more spiritual, more holy, more blameless than I actually am.

Remember — God prefers my honesty to a prayer where I pretend.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 3
texte:
Day 3. God Is There, Even When I Don't Feel Him.

There are seasons when we pray and nothing seems to move. We ask God to intervene, but the heavens seem silent. And in those moments, a thought can quickly settle in: "God has forgotten me… Has God rejected me? Does he still love me? Why doesn't he answer?"

God's silence can be hard to live with, but his silence is not his absence.

Our emotions are real, but they aren't always a reliable indicator of God's presence. I can feel nothing and yet be deeply loved. I can not understand what God is doing and yet be accompanied by him.

On the cross, Jesus himself spoke the words of Psalm 22: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" The Bible shows us that the feeling of abandonment can exist in the very heart of a relationship with God.

In these periods, I must learn to lean more on what God has said than on what I feel. He promised not to abandon me. He has inscribed me on his hands. He walks with me when I pass through waters and fire.

I shouldn't interpret a season of silence as proof of rejection. God remains my Father. His love for me doesn't vary according to my feelings.

And the silence won't always have the last word. God knows when to speak, when to act, and how to lead me. In the meantime, I can choose to believe he is there.

Remember — It's not because I don't feel God that he isn't there.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 4
texte:
Day 4. When My Thoughts Become Too Heavy.

When I'm not doing well, my thoughts can become a second battle.

A situation is already difficult, but my mind sometimes starts to amplify it: "Nothing will change. It's all over. I'll never manage. I'm alone. God has abandoned me." By repeating these phrases over and over internally, I can end up seeing my entire reality through them.

Suffering is real. This isn't about denying it or pretending everything is okay. But not all the thoughts that come from my suffering tell the truth.

The Bible invites me to renew my mind. This doesn't mean spending the day nervously struggling against every negative thought. I can learn to do something simpler: progressively replace the lie with the truth.

When my mind says, "You're alone," I can remind myself: "God will never abandon me." When it says, "There's no future anymore," I can remind myself that God remains the God of hope. When I think, "I'll never manage," I can return to the grace that's sufficient for today.

I also need to pay attention to what I feed myself with. What I listen to, what I watch, and the conversations I expose myself to can feed either worry or peace.

Today, I can identify a thought that's crushing me and search God's Word for a truth that answers it. Then I can return to that truth every time the negative voice comes back.

Remember — Not all my thoughts tell the truth.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 5
texte:
Day 5. Taking Care of My Whole Self.

When we're not feeling well, we sometimes only look for a spiritual cause. Yet God created us as complete beings. The Bible speaks of our body, our soul, and our spirit. These dimensions are connected and all need attention.

First, I have a body. It needs sleep, balanced nutrition, movement, and rest. In Elijah's story, God doesn't begin by giving him a long lecture when he's exhausted. He lets him sleep, gives him food and drink, then sends him on his way. Sometimes, taking care of your body is already part of the answer.

Next, I have a spiritual life. I need to nourish my relationship with God: pray, read his Word, praise, stay in communion with him. When I neglect this relationship for a long time, I can become more vulnerable to emptiness, fear, and discouragement.

Finally, I have a soul, with my thoughts and emotions. They're influenced by what I'm experiencing and what I let in. Certain conversations, certain content, or certain situations can continually feed anxiety and negativity. On the other hand, praise, gratitude, healthy relationships, and times of rest can help my heart breathe.

Taking care of myself isn't selfish and it's not a lack of faith. My body and my inner life are also things God has entrusted to me.

Today, I can simply ask myself: in which area do I need to find a little more balance?

Remember — Taking care of myself means taking care of what God has entrusted to me.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 6
texte:
Day 6. I Don't Need to Fix Everything Today.

When I'm not doing well, I can become even more demanding of myself. I want to understand what's happening to me, find a solution, fix what's wrong, catch up on my backlog, and get back in control. And sometimes I'd like to fix everything today.

But Jesus reminds us that each day already has enough worries of its own.

I can learn to be more compassionate with myself. Some things take time. Some answers won't come today. Some situations don't even depend on me.

I can lay what I can't control at God's feet and breathe.

This doesn't mean abandoning my responsibilities. It means accepting that I'm a human being with limits. I can do what's possible today and leave tomorrow for tomorrow.

Maybe my next step is very simple: to rest, eat well, go for a walk, pray for a few minutes, call someone, finish one single task, or simply sleep.

I don't need to carry today the weight of weeks, months, or years to come. God gives me his grace for today.

So I can breathe. I can slow down. I can stop condemning myself because everything isn't fixed yet.

Today is one day. And with God, one step is enough to begin.

Remember — I don't need to carry today the weight of my entire life.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 7
texte:
Day 7. God Can Lift Me Up.

When we're not doing well, we easily become absolute in our judgments. "This time, it's finished. I'll never get through this. I'll never find peace again."

But what I feel today isn't necessarily a prophecy about tomorrow.

When pain is strong, it narrows our vision. We easily forget the seasons before. Yet if I look back, I can probably find moments when I already thought I couldn't continue. And despite everything, God carried me until now.

The Bible often invites us to remember. Remembering God's past faithfulness can nourish my present hope.

I can remind myself of a door he opened, a prayer he answered, a difficult period he brought me through, a person he placed in my path, or simply the strength he gave me to endure.

And when my own memories become foggy, I can open his Word. It's full of stories of men and women who fell, wept, were afraid, and yet were lifted up.

Being down today doesn't mean I'll stay there.

I may not yet know how God will act. I don't know how long it will take. But I can refuse to declare finished a story that God is still writing.

God has lifted me up before. He can do it again.

Remember — This difficult chapter is not my entire story.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 8
texte:
Day 8. Don't Let Tomorrow Steal Your Today.

It's sometimes difficult to identify why we don't feel well. Yet, part of our inner fatigue comes from things that… haven't even happened yet.

We anticipate. What if it goes wrong? What if I can't do it? What if I lose my job? What if this person leaves me? What if the result is bad? What if tomorrow…?

Our mind builds scenarios, then our body and emotions begin to react as if these scenarios had already become reality. And that's the whole trap of worry: we can suffer today because of a tomorrow that doesn't exist yet.

Most of the things we fear will never happen. And yet, we can lose enormous amounts of energy imagining what could go wrong, mentally reliving situations that don't exist yet, or trying to control events we sometimes have no power over.

Meanwhile, this worry can destroy our present. It steals our energy, disrupts our sleep, feeds our anxiety, and sometimes prevents us from enjoying the good things God places before us today.

Even when my worry concerns something truly possible, I need to ask myself a simple question: can I do something about it today?

If yes, I can do what is within my power. If no, worry won't give me more control.

Jesus actually asks us this question: who can, by worrying, add anything to their life?

Worry sometimes gives us the impression of acting because our mind works endlessly on the problem. But constantly thinking about something I can't control doesn't give me the solution but additional problems.

Preparing for tomorrow is one thing. Living anxiously in tomorrow before it arrives is another.

I can be thoughtful, make necessary decisions, and do what depends on me. But after that, I must learn to place what doesn't depend on me into God's hands. Tomorrow may have its difficulties, but tomorrow will also have God's grace for tomorrow. Today, God gives me the grace I need for today.

So, when my mind begins to imagine everything that could go wrong, I can return to the present and ask myself: "What is really before me today?" I do what I can today. I entrust to God what I can't control. And I refuse to live today the hypothetical suffering of tomorrow.

Remember — Don't let tomorrow's possible problems steal the peace God wants to give you today.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 9
texte:
Day 9. It's Not the End of My Story.

When we suffer, the present can take up all the space. Today's pain becomes so great that we feel it will be there tomorrow, next month, next year, maybe always.

Yet our life on this earth lasts only a time. And our trials, too, are limited.

There are valleys, but there are also peaks. There are seasons of tears and seasons when joy returns. What I'm going through today is part of my story, not all of my story.

And our hope goes even further.

There are situations that may not be resolved the way we would have wanted here on earth. Christian faith doesn't promise us a life without suffering. It gives us something greater: a hope that transcends this life.

One day, those who belong to Jesus will be with him. There will be no more death, no more grief, no more cry, no more pain. God will wipe away every tear.

Paul said that the sufferings of the present time cannot be compared to the glory to come. This doesn't minimize what I'm experiencing. My pain is real and God sees it. But it doesn't have the last word.

I sometimes need to put things in their proper place. This moment is difficult, but this moment is not eternal. This valley is real, but it is not my final destination.

My ultimate future is not suffering. My future is with Jesus.

So I can lift my eyes. Maybe I don't yet see the mountain that comes after this valley. But I know where my story ends: in God's presence.

Remember — What I'm going through is temporary. My hope is eternal.

titre: God, I'm Not Doing Well — Day 10
texte:
Day 10. The Last Meditation, to Close Out….

If you've made it this far, I want you to remember one thing: not feeling well is not a fate, and what you're going through today doesn't define who you are or what your future will be.

There will be seasons in life when everything feels heavier. Moments of tiredness, discouragement, worry, fear, or confusion. Moments when your thoughts might take up too much space and you'll struggle to see beyond what you're feeling.

In those moments, remember that you don't need to pretend in front of God.

You can come to him as you are. You can speak to him freely. You can tell him that you're tired, sad, worried, disappointed, or even angry. You can entrust him with your deepest thoughts, your questions, and your confusion.

God is not afraid of what you feel.

Also learn to take care of yourself in every dimension of your life. Take care of your body, your soul, and your spirit. Guard your thoughts. Nourish yourself with God's Word. Surround yourself with people who do you good. Rest when you need to. And most importantly, don't let tomorrow's worries steal the grace God gives you today.

You don't need to understand everything now. You don't need to solve everything today. You don't need to be strong all the time.

Simply move forward one day at a time, with God.

And when your emotions tell you everything is over, remember what God has already done. Look behind you. Remember the valleys he's already helped you cross. Then look ahead with hope.

Because it's not the end of your story.

This season will pass. And even beyond this life, we have in Jesus an extraordinary hope: that of eternity in his presence, where there will be no more grief, no more cry, no more pain.

So today, even if you're not doing well, keep this small light burning in your heart:

God is there. God loves you. And he can still write very beautiful pages of your story.

With all my affection, Josy W. Brunet

Day 1. God Is with You.

It's not a magic formula—it's a shift in focus. You stop staring at the problem and turn toward the One who's holding your hand.

My friend, I want to tell you with conviction: you are not alone, and you never have been. The God who created the universe promised to be by your side. Move through your day not by clenching your teeth, but by remembering that He walks with you, step by step.

Day 2. A Spirit of Power, Not Fear.

Take back the authority God has given you. Fear hates being contradicted by truth.

I urge you today: don't let an intruder run your life anymore. You don't move forward by your own strength alone—the Spirit of God lives in you. Lift your head; fear will not have the final word over your calling.

Day 3. Perfect Love Casts Out Fear.

My deepest desire is for you to stop living under the pressure to please and to live in the security of being loved. When you know who you are to your Father, the gaze of others loses its power over you. Walk today as a beloved child, not as an accused one who must justify himself.

Day 4. The Lord Is My Light.

And often, what seemed crushing shrinks in His presence.

Your task today: take a sheet of paper or your notebook, write down in black and white what scares you, then write beside it an attribute of God that's greater than that fear—His power, His faithfulness, His love. Confront your fear with His greatness.

I want to encourage you: everything exposed to God's light stops dominating you in secret. Don't stay alone with your fears in the dark. Bring them to the light, and you'll see that they were never as big as they wanted you to believe.

Day 5. Only Believe.

My friend, you've reached the end of this journey on fear, and I want to bless you: may confidence take the place that fear was holding. Believe only. Not perfect faith, but faith turned toward Jesus. It's enough for Him, and it's enough to move your life.

Day 1. Unload It All on Him.

"Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you." Stop on the word "cast." It brings to mind a weight you take off your shoulders. Peter assumes one thing: you're carrying something too heavy. And he's right, isn't he?

Imagine walking all day with a backpack filled with stones: the bills, your children's future, your health, that unresolved conflict. After a while, you don't even feel the weight anymore because you've gotten so used to it, but it's exhausting you. God says to you: "Put that bag down, it's not yours to carry alone."

I need to be honest with you: I'm also tempted to carry everything. Pastor, husband, father, content creator… there are a thousand reasons to worry. But I've learned that worry never fixes tomorrow; it only steals the peace of today. So every morning, I choose to hand my bag over to God.

Here's your assignment, and I want you to actually do it: take your notebook, write down each worry, one by one. Then, before each one, say out loud: "Lord, I entrust this to You." This gesture isn't symbolic—it's spiritual. You're actually transferring the weight to the One who cares for you.

I urge you today: don't pick up the bag you just set down. That's our great temptation—we trust, then we take it back. Leave it in your Father's hands. He's never complained that one of His children trusts Him too much.

Day 2. Worry About Nothing.

Paul writes: "Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God…" And notice what he offers instead of worry: prayer, with thanksgiving. He doesn't say "stop stressing," he gives you a concrete exchange.

Worry and prayer have one thing in common: they both circle around the same problem. The difference is the direction. Worry loops in your head, closed in on itself. Prayer takes that same concern and opens it toward Heaven. Same subject, but a radically different outcome.

I remember nights when my mind replayed the same anxious scenario over and over, again and again. Nothing changed except that I was exhausted. The day I transformed those ruminations into prayer—"Lord, here's what's eating at me"—I felt peace come, not because the situation had changed, but because I was no longer alone in carrying it.

Application for today: the moment a worry rises up, don't let it loop. Transform it into prayer immediately. And add a thank you—thank God for something He's already done. Gratitude disarms anxiety because it reminds your heart that God has already been faithful.

And here's the promise I want you to take with you: "the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts." This peace can't be explained; it must be received. It comes to stand guard over your heart like a soldier. Today, exchange each worry for a prayer, and let that peace take its post.

Day 3. Today Has Enough Trouble of Its Own.

Jesus says: "Do not worry about tomorrow… each day has enough trouble of its own." Have you noticed that most of our anxiety isn't about today, but tomorrow? "What if…?" That's the phrase that opens the door to a thousand scenarios that, most often, will never happen.

Let me give you a picture. God gives us grace like the manna in the desert: one portion for each day, not a reserve in advance. The Israelites who wanted to store manna for the next day found it spoiled. Why? Because God wanted to teach them to depend on Him one day at a time.

That's exactly why you feel crushed when you imagine tomorrow: you're trying to face today battles for which God hasn't yet given you the grace. You have the strength for this day, not for the twenty scenarios your imagination invents.

Here's your exercise: bring yourself back to today. Just ask yourself "What is the one next step I can take right now?" and take it. Not the ten that follow, just that one. Trust the rest to God, who will be there tomorrow with fresh grace.

I want to encourage you with all my heart: you don't have to carry tomorrow today. God is already waiting for you in your tomorrow, and He will have placed there exactly what you'll need. Live today fully—it's the only day when you have the grace to act.

Day 4. The Peace the World Cannot Give.

"Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives." Jesus distinguishes between two kinds of peace. The world's peace depends on circumstances: everything is fine as long as nothing goes wrong. His is of another nature entirely: it's a peace of presence, not the absence of problems.

The world offers you peace by eliminating everything that disturbs you, or by distracting you so you stop thinking about it. That's why we fill our silences with screens: as long as we're busy, we don't hear the anxiety. But this kind of peace evaporates the moment you turn off the screen. It calms the surface without touching the heart.

Jesus doesn't ask you to run away. He comes with you in the storm. Think of the disciples in the boat tossed by the waves: even before the sea had calmed, Jesus was already there, present. His peace isn't a calm sea—it's His presence in the boat.

Today, I invite you to a time of real silence, no phone, no music, no noise. Five minutes. Instead of running from what you feel, bring it to Jesus and simply say: "Give me Your peace, the kind the world cannot give." Stay there, and receive it.

My friend, don't settle for the world's painkillers. They numb; they don't heal. Receive the peace of Jesus, the kind that holds firm even when everything trembles around you. It's a gift, not a reward: you don't have to earn it, just receive it.

Day 5. Rest for Your Soul.

"Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest." If you've made it this far in this journey, maybe it's because you're tired. Not just physically—tired on the inside. And Jesus is addressing this invitation personally to you.

Look closely: He doesn't say "fix your problems first, then come." He says "come," period. He's not asking you to arrive rested; He's asking you to arrive tired. Rest isn't the condition for coming to Him; it's the gift He gives you when you do.

Jesus speaks of a "yoke." In His time, they often yoked a young ox next to an older, more experienced ox, who carried the real weight and set the direction. When Jesus says "take my yoke upon you," He's saying: "walk yoked to me, let me carry the weight and show you the pace." Anxiety often comes from trying to pull everything alone.

Very practical application to close this journey: choose one area where you've been pulling all by yourself for too long, and invite Jesus to carry it with you. Tell Him: "I don't want to go forward alone in this anymore. Walk with me." Then adjust your pace to His, not the other way around.

I want to bless you as you finish these five days: may you find true rest for your soul, not just a temporary reprieve. Anxiety told you to carry everything; Jesus tells you to come. Lay your burden at His feet today, and learn from Him that gentle, light pace for which you were created.

Day 1. Faith Comes from God's Word.

"Faith comes from hearing, and what is heard comes through God's Word." Here's a truth that sets you free: faith is not a gift reserved for a privileged few, nor is it an act of will you have to force. Faith is nourished. It grows when it is exposed to the right food: God's Word.

Think of a fire. You can blow on it with all your might, but if you don't add wood, it will eventually go out. Many Christians try to "force themselves to believe" while they never feed the flame. They pray for more faith, but never give their faith anything to strengthen it.

I can testify to this: the seasons when my faith was strongest were not those when I felt most inspired, but those when I was most nourished by God's Word. When I neglect the Word, my faith shrinks, almost without me noticing. When I fill myself with it, confidence returns naturally.

Application for today: don't just speed-read a verse. Take today's verse, read it aloud, several times, slowly. Let it move from your head to your heart. Faith doesn't enter through quick reading, but through meditation that lingers.

I encourage you to make God's Word your nourishment, not your supplement. You wouldn't ask "do I need to eat today?"—your body demands its food. Let your soul learn to demand its own. Give your faith something to grow on, and you'll be amazed at how it strengthens.

Day 2. Walking by Faith.

"We walk by faith and not by sight." Notice the word "walk." Paul doesn't say "we dream by faith" or "we talk about faith." Faith is movement, a concrete step. And walking by faith often means moving forward before you've seen, understood, or mastered everything.

When you climb stairs in the dark, you don't see all the steps. You put your foot on the first one trusting there will be a second. Faith works like this: God rarely lights the entire path at once. He lights the next step and asks you to take it before showing you the one after.

I know what I'm talking about. When God pushed me to take the leap, I had no complete plan, no guarantee, no proof it would work. I had a conviction and one first step to take. If I had waited to see everything clearly, I never would have started. Clarity came through walking, not through sitting still.

Here's your application: identify a place where God is asking you to move forward, but you're waiting for all guarantees. And take the first reasonable step you can take today, leaning on His character rather than on what you see.

Let me encourage you: don't let the need to control everything suffocate what God wants to do through you. Faith accepts not having full control, because it knows the One who holds the path. Move forward. You'll discover that ground appears beneath your feet as you step.

Day 3. All Things Are Possible to Him Who Believes.

"All things are possible to him who believes," says Jesus. And the father's response is one of the most honest prayers in all of Scripture: "I believe; help my unbelief!" This man believes and doubts at the same time, and Jesus acts anyway. What a relief.

Many Christians remain paralyzed because they think they need perfect faith, without a trace of doubt, for God to act. But look at this text: Jesus doesn't demand flawless faith. He responds to honest faith, even mixed with questions, as long as it turns toward Him.

I want to be transparent with you: I still doubt sometimes. There are prayers where I believe strongly, and others where I whisper "Lord, help me believe." And I've seen God answer in both cases. What matters is not the perfection of my faith, but its direction—toward Him.

Application for today: stop waiting to "feel" enough faith before coming to God. Come as you are, with your faith and doubts mixed together. Pray like that father: "I believe, Lord; help my unbelief." And bring Him what you've stopped daring to hope for.

My friend, don't disqualify your faith because it seems too small to you. Jesus said that faith as small as a mustard seed is enough to move a mountain. It's not the size of your faith that makes the difference—it's the greatness of the One in whom you place it. Bring Him your small faith; it's in very capable hands.

Day 4. The Faith That Pleases God.

"Without faith it is impossible to please Him." That's a powerful statement. Why does faith matter so much to God? Because believing honors Him as He deserves: it means holding Him to be faithful, true, and good. Constant doubt about Him subtly questions His character.

Think of a human relationship. Nothing hurts a faithful person more than being constantly suspected. Conversely, trusting someone worthy of trust honors them. When you believe God at His word, you're telling Him: "I know You are good, even when I don't understand." And that touches His heart.

The verse adds that God "rewards those who seek Him." So faith is not passive; it seeks. It moves toward God. In my life, the times when I truly sought God—not out of habit but with hunger—have always been times when my faith grew and He allowed Himself to be found.

Application: today, choose to believe that God is good, especially in the area where you have the most reason to doubt. Seek Him deliberately, through prayer, His Word, worship. Give Him time, the way you'd spend time with someone you truly want to know.

I encourage you to move from distrust to confidence. God is not a distant Father waiting for you to stumble; He is a good Father who rewards those who seek Him. Honor Him today with your trust, and you'll discover a God far more faithful than your fears led you to believe.

Day 5. Persevering Through Trials.

"Consider it pure joy when you face trials of many kinds, knowing that the testing of your faith develops perseverance." I know this verse can be hard to hear when you're suffering. James isn't saying to rejoice in the trial itself, but in what it can produce if you walk through it with God.

A tree exposed to wind develops deeper roots than one protected from everything. Muscles only strengthen under resistance. This is a law God has written even into nature: true growth often comes through difficulty. Your faith becomes solid only through being tested.

I can tell you plainly: the deepest lessons of my life, I didn't learn on the mountaintops but in the valleys. The hardest seasons were when my trust in God took deepest root. In the moment, I saw only the pain. With hindsight, I see what God was building.

Application as we close this journey: don't waste your trial. Instead of only asking "Lord, make this stop," add "Lord, what do You want to grow in me through this?" Look for God's work, not just the exit.

My friend, as you finish these five days, I want to bless you: may your faith, tested, emerge purer and stronger than before. God never wastes pain entrusted into His hands. Persevere. What you're walking through is not the end of your faith—it may be the ground where it becomes unshakeable.

titre: Filled with the Holy Spirit — Day 1
texte:
Day 1. The Promise of the Counselor.

Before leaving His disciples, Jesus makes them a staggering promise: "I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Counselor, that He may abide with you forever." Picture the scene: they fear losing Jesus, and He announces to them a presence that will never leave them.

The word translated as "Counselor" refers to someone called to your side to help, defend, and encourage. The Holy Spirit is not a vague energy or an impersonal force. He is God Himself, come to dwell in you. Let this truth seize you: God doesn't just stand with you—He chooses to live in you.

For a long time, I lived my faith as though God were distant, somewhere far off in heaven, and I had to shout to be heard. The day I realized His Spirit actually lived in me, my relationship with Him changed. I no longer had to search for Him afar; He was already there, closer than my own breath.

Application for today: take a moment, place your hand on your heart if it helps, and simply say: "Thank you, Holy Spirit, for dwelling in me." Then rest in that silence for a few minutes, aware that He is there. Not to feel something extraordinary, just to acknowledge His presence.

I want you to carry this truth all day long: you are never alone, never. Wherever you go, whatever you face, the Counselor is with you and in you. Learn to live conscious of His presence, and your entire day becomes a walk for two.

titre: Filled with the Holy Spirit — Day 2
texte:
Day 2. Power from on High.

"You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you; and you will be My witnesses." Just before these words, the disciples were fearful men, locked away, who had abandoned Jesus. Days later, filled with the Spirit, these same men proclaim the Gospel without fear before crowds. What changed? Power from on high.

There is a Christian life you try to live by your own strength, and there is a Christian life lived by the power of the Spirit. The first exhausts you; the second bears fruit. Many believers are tired because they attempt to do with their muscles what God wants to do through His Spirit.

I see it constantly in ministry: what I accomplish by my own abilities remains small, but what I do in dependence on the Spirit far exceeds what I'm capable of. That power isn't there to make us impressive; it's there to make us witnesses, to love and announce Jesus beyond our limits.

Application for today: before your day begins, explicitly ask to be filled with the Spirit. Say: "Holy Spirit, I don't want to move forward on my own strength today. Fill me, work through me." Then expect Him to open an opportunity to speak of Jesus, or to love someone you wouldn't have loved alone.

I urge you not to settle for a powerless faith. God never intended for you to live depleted. There is fullness available to you. Ask for it, expect it, and let the Spirit do through your life what you could never accomplish alone.

titre: Filled with the Holy Spirit — Day 3
texte:
Day 3. Led by the Spirit.

"As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God." The Holy Spirit doesn't just dwell in you—He wants to lead you. And notice the word "led," not "pushed" or "forced." God doesn't drag you like a slave; He guides you like a shepherd guides his sheep, with gentleness.

The problem is we often expect spectacular signs, when the Spirit speaks most often through quiet means: a deep peace in a direction, a hesitation that holds you back, a verse that suddenly resonates, a gentle but persistent conviction. Learning to recognize His voice means learning to recognize these subtle touches.

In my own life, the best decisions I've made didn't come from a thunderbolt, but from a quiet peace that settled in when I moved the right way, and unease when I drifted away. I had to learn to slow down to hear that gentle voice that the noise of my life too often drowned out.

Application for today: slow down. Before any decision, even a small one, take a moment to ask: "Holy Spirit, how do You want to lead me here?" Then be attentive to the peace or unease within. Learn to follow His direction in small things, and you'll know how to follow Him in great ones.

My friend, you don't have to figure your life out alone. You have a perfect Guide living in you. But a gentle voice is only heard by those who take time to listen. Make listening to the Spirit a habit, and you'll walk with an assurance the world cannot understand.

titre: Filled with the Holy Spirit — Day 4
texte:
Day 4. The Fruit of the Spirit.

"The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control." Notice well: Paul doesn't speak of the "works" of the Spirit, but of His "fruit." And fruit doesn't grow by sheer willpower—it grows naturally.

An apple tree doesn't grit its teeth and strain to produce apples. It bears fruit naturally because it's alive and connected to its roots. That's the image Jesus uses: "abide in Me." The character of Christ isn't produced by effort, but by connection. Stay rooted in the source, and fruit comes.

I must be honest: for a time, I tried to be patient, gentle, loving—by discipline. And I failed, again and again. It was only when I stopped trying to "produce" and started to "connect" that I saw these qualities begin to grow in me. The fruit was the result of communion, not effort.

Application for today: choose just one aspect of this fruit—the one you need most right now (patience? gentleness? self-control?). And instead of telling yourself "I'm going to force this," ask the Spirit: "Produce this fruit in me," then stay connected to Him today in small moments.

I encourage you to stop exhausting yourself by imitating Jesus from the outside, and let Him transform you from the inside. The fruit of the Spirit isn't a checklist of resolutions; it's the portrait of Jesus slowly emerging in a life connected to Him. Abide in Him, and you will grow to resemble Him more and more.

titre: Filled with the Holy Spirit — Day 5
texte:
Day 5. Praying in the Spirit.

"The Spirit Himself helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words." What a liberating verse to close this journey. It contradicts the lie that says you must be strong and know perfectly how to pray to draw near to God.

There are moments when you don't know what to say to God anymore. Your heart is too heavy, words won't come, you sit there, empty. Paul tells us: that's precisely when the Spirit steps in. When you've run out of words, He prays for you, in you, better than you ever could.

I remember seasons when my prayer was nothing but tears and silence. I felt guilty for not praying "correctly." Then I understood: those wordless sighs were perhaps the deepest prayers of my life, because it was the Spirit praying through my weakness. God didn't need my polished phrases, just my open heart.

Application for today: don't avoid prayer under the excuse that you wouldn't know what to say. Simply present yourself to God, even without words. You can pray this way: "Holy Spirit, I don't know how to pray about this. Pray in me, in my place." Then rest in His presence, in trust.

My friend, as you finish these five days, hold onto this: you never have to come before God pretending to be strong. Your weakness is not an obstacle to prayer—it's the place where the Spirit works most powerfully. Lean on Him, let Him carry you, and your prayer life will enter a new depth.

Day 1. Child of God.

"To all who received Him, He gave the power to become children of God." Before talking about what you do, God wants to settle the question of what you are. And the first thing He declares about the one who receives Jesus is: "you are My child." Not My employee, not My project, My child.

The world teaches us to build our identity on our performances: you're worth what you produce, what you achieve, what others think of you. It's an exhausting race with no finish line. God proposes the opposite: an identity received, not earned. You don't have to become someone good to be loved; you are loved, and that's where you can live from.

I searched for that worth elsewhere for a long time. In recognition, in results, in approval. And the more I sought it, the more it slipped away. The day I really received that I was a loved child of the Father, I stopped begging for what I already possessed. It changes everything, believe me.

Application for today: every time you catch yourself wanting to prove your worth, at work, on social media, in your relationships, stop and declare: "I have nothing to prove. I am already God's child." Live this day from that identity, not to obtain it.

My friend, receive today what your Father declares over you. You are not a number, not an accident, not a disappointment. You are His child, loved, wanted, chosen. Let your whole life flow from this source: not "I must be loved," but "I am loved."

Day 2. A New Creation.

"If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. Old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." This is one of the most beautiful pieces of good news in the Gospel: your past does not have the final say over your future. In Jesus, you are not a repaired version of the old you, you are brand new.

The enemy loves to pull you backward. He reminds you of your failures, your sins, what you did or what was done to you, to convince you that you will always be "like that." It's a lie. God does not define you by your worst day. He defines you by what Christ did for you.

I have seen lives that everyone thought were ruined be completely transformed by Jesus. People trapped in addictions, wounds, shame, becoming free and radiant. If God could do that for them, He can do it for you. No story is too broken for His grace.

Application for today: take a label you still wear—"I'm worthless," "I'm broken," "I will always be this way"—and consciously replace it with the truth: "in Christ, I am a new creation." Refuse to keep wearing a name that God has already taken from you.

I want to encourage you with all my strength: don't let your past write your future. What you were yesterday is not what you are today in Jesus. Rise up in your new identity. The old has passed away; God is making all things new in you, and He's not finished.

Day 3. Chosen and Loved.

"In Him, God chose us before the foundation of the world… predestining us to adoption as His children." Read that slowly: before the world even existed, before you were born, before you did anything good or bad, God had already chosen you. You are not an afterthought in God's heart.

Many carry deep down the feeling of being "too much," of not really having a place. Maybe you've known rejection, abandonment, the impression that you have to justify your existence. This verse comes to heal that wound at the root: you have been desired for all eternity by a Father who chose you knowingly.
