A couple celebrating their wedding anniversary doesn't just reminisce: by repeating the gestures of love—the meal, the words, sometimes the place—they renew their present commitment. That is what the Church does at the Lord's table: it renews the covenant, “till He comes.”

Notice also to whom Paul writes these lines: to the church at Corinth, a community full of divisions, disorder, and scandals—not an assembly of perfect people. And he doesn't tell them, “Stop taking Communion until further notice,” but “Take it in a worthy manner.” The Lord's table has always been set in the midst of imperfect churches: it is not the reward of the blameless; it is the meeting place of the redeemed.

One last detail that gives you chills: “the Lord Jesus, ON THE SAME NIGHT IN WHICH HE WAS BETRAYED, took bread… and gave thanks.” He knew—Judas had already gone out into the night—and He gave thanks. Facing the worst night in history, Jesus opened His hands and gave thanks. Every Communion teaches us this way of walking through our own nights.

titre: The Lord's Supper — The Meaning of Holy Communion
texte:
The Meaning of the Lord's Supper

Like baptism, the Lord's Supper invites us to look to the cross where Jesus gave His life: the bread represents His crucified body, and the wine recalls His shed blood. By partaking of them, Christians remember the price Jesus paid for their redemption: His death. They also proclaim His resurrection, for they partake while awaiting His return and the feast of the Lamb.

“For I say to you, I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes… that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” (Luke 22:18, 30; see also Revelation 19:9)

The Lord's Supper is not merely a symbol. It calls upon our faith. It is by faith that we know Jesus is present among us and that we experience real fellowship with our brothers and sisters in Jesus. It is also through our faith that the Holy Spirit enables us to take full possession of everything the Lord obtained for us by dying on the cross for us: our forgiveness, our healing, our deliverance.

“But He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement for our peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:5)

The Bible never speaks of a miracle in which the substance of the elements changes at the moment of the celebration. The bread and the wine remain what they are, but at the same time they bear witness to a living reality that goes beyond them: Jesus, who died and rose again, truly present and alive in us and among us.

The Bible gives no further details about celebrating the Lord's Supper, such as its frequency, its manner, or its date. Each church is therefore called to adapt its practice to its context, according to the deep meaning of the Lord's Supper that it perceives and that governs the practical aspects. It would therefore be a mistake to judge Christians who practice it somewhat differently from us, for life with God is above all a matter of love, obedience, and faith. The Lord's Supper is a means to help us in that. It is not an end in itself.

Notice God's way of teaching: He could have simply asked us to think about the cross. Instead, He chose a meal, which engages all the senses—the bread you hold, break, and taste; the cup you bring to your lips. God knows our nature: we are not pure spirits, and truths that pass through the body are imprinted more deeply than those that remain ideas. That is why the Lord's Supper also reaches those going through seasons when they don't “feel” anything: even when emotion is absent, the act proclaims, and faith leans on the act.

Note the biblical balance between two extremes. On one hand, the Lord's Supper is not a magical act in which the bread changes substance—the Bible never speaks of such a miracle. On the other, it is not merely an empty memory, a ceremony of the past: Paul speaks of “the communion of the blood of Christ… the communion of the body of Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:16)—the Greek word is koinōnia, a real participation. By faith, the Risen One is present and active at His table: forgiveness sealed, hearts healed, relationships restored.

And don't forget which way to look: the Lord's Supper looks back (to the cross), around (to the brothers and sisters with whom we share the same bread—“we, though many, are one body; for we all partake of that one bread,” 1 Corinthians 10:17), and FORWARD: “till He comes.” Every Communion is a dress rehearsal for the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Around the table, the Church has its back turned to Egypt and its face turned toward the Kingdom.

titre: The Lord's Supper — Taking the Lord's Supper Unworthily
texte:
Taking the Lord's Supper Unworthily

The biblical term “communion” also shows that the Lord's Supper cannot be taken lightly: it bears witness to our communion with God and with our brothers and sisters. The apostle Paul speaks of the possibility of taking the Lord's Supper “in an unworthy manner.” What do you think that means?

It would be wrong to take part in this meal if we are not in genuine communion with God and with one another. That is what was happening in Corinth: “For in eating, each one takes his own supper ahead of others; and one is hungry and another is drunk.” (1 Corinthians 11:21)

“Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For he who eats and drinks without discerning the Lord's body eats and drinks judgment to himself. For this reason many are weak and sick among you, and many sleep.” (1 Corinthians 11:27-30)

“Therefore if you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matthew 5:23-24)

Yet it would be a serious mistake to keep depriving yourself of Holy Communion without seeking to make things right with God and with your brothers and sisters. God wants us to remember the price of our salvation: His love revealed through Jesus' sacrifice on the cross.

What attitudes should fill a Christian's heart when taking part in Holy Communion? “Love does not behave rudely, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil.” (1 Corinthians 13:5)

One word here sets many anxious Christians free: Paul speaks of taking the Lord's Supper “unworthily”—in an unworthy manner. It's an adverb, describing a way of doing something, not an adjective describing unworthy people. After all, who could ever be “worthy” of Christ's sacrifice? No one. The Lord's table isn't set for the perfect, but for forgiven sinners. If you wait until you're worthy to come, you'll never come; if you understand that it's for those hungry for grace, you'll run to it.

In Corinth, the problem wasn't that imperfect people were taking part: it was that people were taking part without love. Picture the scene: the Lord's Supper was shared during a real community meal. The wealthy, arriving early, ate and drank among themselves to the point of drunkenness, while the slaves and laborers, arriving late, found the dishes empty and went hungry—and then everyone “celebrated” the memorial of the One who gave His body for all. That is the unworthiness Paul condemns: approaching the sacrifice of love while trampling on your brothers and sisters.

Self-examination, then, is a mirror, not a barrier. Before Communion, ask yourself two simple questions: Am I at peace with God? Am I at peace with my brothers and sisters? If there's a grudge, a conflict, a word that needs to be made right—first go and be reconciled, Jesus says, then come. Many churches have seen real reconciliations happen precisely because Communion was coming up: brothers estranged for months finally talking on Sunday morning. It's one of its most precious fruits—the Lord's table cleans house in our relationships like nothing else.

And if, on the other hand, you find yourself avoiding Communion month after month out of a sense of unworthiness: now is the time to talk with a leader. Staying away from the remedy because you know you're sick is the exact opposite of the Gospel.

Conclusion

Holy Communion is far more than a mere rite or Christian tradition: it is an invitation to remember, to proclaim, and to live in communion with Jesus Christ and with our brothers and sisters. As we share the bread and the wine, we recall Jesus' ultimate sacrifice on the cross, His body given and His blood shed for the forgiveness of our sins. This act, filled with faith and love, brings us back to what matters most: the grace of God, the power of the cross, and the hope of His return.

It is also a call to self-examination and reconciliation. The Lord's Supper reminds us that our communion with God cannot be separated from our communion with others. Taking part in this meal in a spirit of faith, gratitude, and reconciliation allows us to fully experience the power of Christ's work in our lives.

So Holy Communion is not simply a moment of quiet reflection, but a living experience of Christ's presence among us. By obeying this command of the Lord, we affirm our devotion to Him, our gratitude for His sacrifice, and our desire to walk in His light until His glorious return.

titre: Tithes and Offerings — Definition and origin of the tithe
texte:
Definition and Origin of the Tithe

The word tithe literally means “tenth part.” The first mention of the tithe in the Bible appears when Abraham chooses to offer it to God in gratitude for the victory He gave him over his enemies:

“And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand! And Abraham gave him a tithe of all.” (Genesis 14:20)

Later, after the dream of the ladder, Jacob vows to give God a tenth of everything he will receive from Him:

“Then Jacob made a vow, saying, If God will be with me, and keep me in this way that I am going, and give me bread to eat and clothing to put on, so that I come back to my father's house in peace, then the Lord shall be my God. And this stone which I have set as a pillar shall be God's house, and of all that You give me I will surely give a tenth to You.” (Genesis 28:20-22)

Later still, in the Law given to Israel, the tithe was established as a divine command:

“You shall truly tithe all the increase of your grain that the field produces year by year. And you shall eat before the Lord your God, in the place where He chooses to make His name abide, the tithe of your grain and your new wine and your oil, of the firstborn of your herds and your flocks, that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always.” (Deuteronomy 14:22-23)

Let's make it very concrete: the tithe is one tenth. On an income of $1,500, that's $150; on $800, it's $80. The principle has a particular beauty: it's proportional, so the same step of trust is asked of everyone, whatever their standard of living.

But pause on one decisive detail: the first two tithes in the Bible—Abraham's and Jacob's—were given BEFORE the Law, centuries before Moses. No one required it of them; no command existed yet. Abraham gives a tithe to Melchizedek in response to a victory God had just given him; Jacob promises it in response to a promise God had just made him. So the tithe is born as a reflex of gratitude, not as a tax—and that's why it spans the ages: it doesn't belong to the system of the Law, it belongs to the grammar of a grateful heart.

The second detail is the word “firstfruits”: the first fruits, not the leftovers. Israel brought the first sheaf of the harvest—before knowing what the rest of the field would yield. Giving first or giving what's left: those are two opposing theologies. The first says, “God is my priority and my security”; the second, “God will get whatever my expenses happen to leave Him.” Here's a test that doesn't lie: look at a bank statement and a calendar—better than any speech, they reveal what holds first place in a life. Jesus put it in one sentence: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Notice the order: He doesn't say your money will follow your heart, but that your heart will follow your money. Put your treasure in the Kingdom, and your heart will hold fast to it.

The Reasons for the Tithe in the Old Testament

1. Acknowledging God’s sovereignty. By giving the tithe, believers acknowledge that everything comes from God: health, work, family, prosperity.

2. Trusting God. Giving a portion of one’s resources, even in difficult circumstances, shows complete dependence on God.

“Bring all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be food in My house, and try Me now in this, says the Lord of hosts, if I will not open for you the windows of heaven and pour out for you such blessing that there will not be room enough to receive it.” (Malachi 3:10-12)

3. Supporting the service of God. The tithe was used to sustain the Levites, the men consecrated to God’s service, and to support worship. When there was slackness, God’s servants abandoned their ministry, and idolatry took hold (2 Chronicles 29:9).

titre: Tithes and Offerings — Freewill offerings and generosity
texte:
Freewill Offerings and Generosity

In addition to the tithe, God encouraged His people to give freely as their hearts moved them. These offerings were used for specific projects, such as building the tabernacle or the temple (Exodus 35:21-29). These seasons of generosity often coincided with spiritual revivals, when the people rediscovered the joy of worshiping and serving God.

Generosity toward the poor: the Mosaic Law included specific instructions for helping those most in need, encouraging generosity and preventing poverty from taking root among the people.

“Six years you shall sow your land and gather in its produce, but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave, the beasts of the field may eat.” (Exodus 23:10-11)

Jesus and the Tithe

Jesus did not abolish the tithe, but He invited His disciples to go beyond it, teaching them to give with a sincere heart.

“Jesus sat opposite the treasury and saw how the people put money into the treasury. And many who were rich put in much. Then one poor widow came and threw in two mites… Jesus said: This poor widow has put in more than all, for she put in all that she had, her whole livelihood.” (Mark 12:41-44)

The scene of the widow overturns our calculations. Picture yourself in the temple: the offering boxes were large, trumpet-shaped metal receptacles, and the coins rang out inside them — the bigger the gift, the louder it sounded. The rich made their offerings ring; a widow slips in two lepta, the smallest coins in existence, barely a clink. And Jesus, sitting across from it, calls His disciples over: she has given “more than all.” Why? Because God doesn’t count what we give, but what we keep: the rich gave out of their surplus; she gave “her whole livelihood.” God looks at what’s left, not at the amount.

Notice too what this scene reveals: Jesus watches what people give — and He isn’t embarrassed by it. Our culture considers money the most private subject there is; Jesus talks about it more often than about prayer, precisely because nothing reveals the heart better.

Let’s correct a widespread distortion here: giving is not a business transaction with God. We don’t “pay” God to get blessings, like putting a coin in a vending machine — those who preach this turn grace into commerce. The promises of Malachi 3 are real: God honors faithfulness, and generations of Christians testify to it. But the meaning of Christian giving is gratitude, not calculation: we give because we have already received everything in Christ — “He who did not spare His own Son… how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). You don’t bribe a Father who has already given everything.

titre: Tithes and Offerings — The Christian and his offering
texte:
The Christian and Their Offering

The offering is an integral part of Christian worship. It would be inconsistent for a believer under grace to give less than under the Law. God was infinitely generous in giving His Son for us:

“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich.” (2 Corinthians 8:9)

The giver’s attitude: the Christian should give joyfully and without compulsion.

“So let each one give as he purposes in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7)

“But when you do a charitable deed, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.” (Matthew 6:3-4)

A piece of advice proven by many Christians: decide in advance, then automate. Paul already gave the Corinthians this plan: “On the first day of the week let each one of you lay something aside, storing up as he may prosper” (1 Corinthians 16:2) — a regular rhythm, a set portion, right from the start. In practical terms today: set up an automatic transfer on the day your income arrives, before your account melts away over the month. This doesn’t take the heart out of the gesture; it protects it: the decision was made in prayer, once, calmly; carrying it out no longer depends on moods or surprises.

And what about difficult financial seasons? Look at the Macedonians, whom Paul praises: “In a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded in the riches of their liberality. For I bear witness that according to their ability, yes, and beyond their ability, they were freely willing” (2 Corinthians 8:2-3). Poor people joyful to give — that shatters the idea that generosity is reserved for the rich. The Bible asks no one to go into debt in order to give; but it shows that the joy of giving doesn’t depend on your balance. Even a small gift, given faithfully in hard times, is an act of faith that says: “My security isn’t my account, it’s my Father.”

Finally, keep the compass of 2 Corinthians 9:7: “not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.” If your gift is being wrung out of you by guilt or pressure, stop, and bring the question back before God until the joy returns: He prefers a smaller gift given joyfully to a large one given reluctantly.

The Tithe: An Act of Worship

Giving the tithe is an act of gratitude and faith:

— An act of faith: the one who gives acknowledges that God will provide for all their needs.

— Support for the work of the Church: tithes and offerings enable the Church to function and to support missionary work around the world.

— A source of joy and praise: “They glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal sharing with them.” (2 Corinthians 9:13)

A key to understanding why money is such a spiritual subject: your money is your life’s time, crystallized. Those hours of work, that fatigue, those skills — all of it has been converted into numbers in an account. So giving money is literally giving part of your life. That’s why the offering given on Sunday isn’t just a line item in the service: it is an act of worship just as much as singing — perhaps even more demanding, because singing costs nothing.

David said something on this subject that should be engraved on our wallets. When he is offered Araunah’s threshing floor for free to build an altar, he refuses: “Nor will I offer burnt offerings to the Lord my God with that which costs me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24). Worship that costs nothing says something about how much we value God. By contrast, Mary of Bethany breaks over Jesus a perfume worth a year’s wages — the disciples cry waste, and Jesus declares that her act will be told throughout the whole world (Mark 14:3-9). Worship gladly “wastes” itself on the one it loves: just ask anyone in love.

And remember who you got what you give from. David again, on the day of the offerings for the temple: “All things come from You, and of Your own we have given You” (1 Chronicles 29:14). Giving doesn’t impoverish the giver: it puts them back in the truth — a richly blessed steward of a generous God who owns it all.

titre: Tithes and Offerings — The example of the early Church
texte:
The Example of the Early Church

The Church of the first Christians was marked by great generosity and true fellowship:

“Now all who believed were together, and had all things in common, and sold their possessions and goods, and divided them among all, as anyone had need.” (Acts 2:44-47)

This generosity is no distant utopia: it is still lived out today. In our churches, it has a thousand concrete faces — meals brought to a mom who just gave birth, a quiet collection to cover the bill of an unemployed brother, a car lent, a home opened to a student. And the text of Acts notes the result: “the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved.” The generosity of the first Christians was their best sermon: the world couldn’t explain these people.

History confirmed it spectacularly: in the fourth century, Emperor Julian — nicknamed the Apostate, who wanted to restore paganism — complained in a now-famous letter that the “impious Galileans” fed not only their own poor but the pagans’ poor as well, putting his religion to shame. The enemy of Christianity unwittingly testified to its greatest proof. No argument has ever converted as many people as the generosity of Christians.

Finally, notice the balance of the text: “they sold their possessions AS ANYONE HAD NEED” — it was neither mandatory communism (Peter would tell Ananias that his field remained his own, Acts 5:4) nor every man for himself: a joyful freedom guided by real needs. That’s the model: not a percentage that settles our duty, but eyes open to the needs around us, and hands that follow.

Conclusion

Tithes and offerings are much more than a mere religious practice: they are an act of worship, faith, and gratitude toward God. By giving, we affirm that everything we own comes from Him, and we express our trust in His ability to provide for all our needs.

These gifts support the work of the Church, foster unity and fellowship among believers, and make it possible to meet the needs of those most in need. As Jesus taught, true giving isn’t measured by quantity, but by the sincerity of the heart.

By embracing the spirit of generosity that characterized the early Church, we bear witness to God’s goodness and to the impact of His grace in our lives. Giving joyfully and in love is a concrete way to glorify God and to take part in the advancement of His Kingdom.

“Bring all the tithes into the storehouse… and I will pour out for you such blessing in abundance.” (Malachi 3:10-12)

titre: The Church — The Universal Church / The Local Church
texte:
The universal Church / the local church

The word church, as it is used in the New Testament, never refers to a building or a place of worship. It is used with two distinct meanings that are important to tell apart.

The universal Church gathers all believers of all times and all places who have put their faith in Jesus Christ. Invisible today, it is known to God alone.

“Nevertheless the solid foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are His.” (2 Timothy 2:19)

The Church as the bride of Christ: the Church is called the Bride of the Lamb. She will be presented to Christ pure, without blemish, and glorious. (Ephesians 5:27; Revelation 21:9)

An old image says it all: take an ember out of the fire and set it alone on a stone — within minutes it blackens and goes out. Put it back among the others, and it glows again. No Christian is made to burn alone. The “churchless Christianity” that our individualistic age finds so appealing is a modern invention the New Testament knows nothing about: from Pentecost on, to believe is to be added to a community (Acts 2:41) — on the very same day, the three thousand converts are baptized AND brought in.

And consider what the Church means in God's eyes, because our idea of it is often far too small. Paul dares to write that Christ “loved the church and gave Himself for her” (Ephesians 5:25) — the Church is what Jesus purchased with His own blood (Acts 20:28). She is His bride, prepared for a wedding (Revelation 19:7). When someone says, “Jesus, yes; the Church, no thanks,” what they are really saying is, “You, yes; Your bride, no” — imagine how a groom would take that. And to Saul, who was persecuting Christians, the risen Lord did not say, “Why are you persecuting My disciples?” but “Why are you persecuting ME?” (Acts 9:4): to touch the Church is to touch Him. You cannot love Christ and despise what He loved at the cost of His life.

And let's settle this once and for all: the church is not the building. You can tear down the building, and the Church remains; you can fill the building, and there may be no Church at all. The Church is redeemed people — and you are one of them.

Jesus, head of the Church

“And He is the head of the body, the church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things He may have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18)

“You are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)

Believers as living stones: the universal Church is a spiritual building that Jesus has been building since Pentecost, transcending human barriers and divisions. It is faith in Christ that unites us to this Church, not our membership in a particular denomination.

“Praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved.” (Acts 2:47)

This truth has a very practical consequence: the Church belongs to no one but Jesus. It does not belong to the pastor, who is only its shepherd under the Chief Shepherd; it does not belong to the founding members, or the longest-standing, or the most generous donors. “I will build MY church,” says Jesus. This protects the Church from abuses of power — no one has the right to make it their property — and it brings reassurance in the storms: the One who builds never fails.

History is its finest commentary. This promise — “the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it” — was spoken before twelve men with no money, no degrees, no influence, in a remote province of the Empire. Since then, the Roman Empire that persecuted the Church has vanished, and the Church is still here; the totalitarian regimes of the twentieth century vowed to destroy it — in the Soviet Union, in Albania, in China — and wherever the buildings were shut down, the Church grew in homes. Today it is found in every nation on earth, and it has never had so many members. No human institution has survived two thousand years of assault: that's because the builder is not human.

Application for our communities: since He is the head, the decisive question in church decisions is never “What do I like?” or “What have we always done?” but “What does the Head want?” A healthy church is a church that asks Jesus' opinion — through the Word and prayer — before it votes.

Local churches

Local churches are the visible and imperfect expressions of the universal Church. They are gatherings of Jesus' disciples in a specific place for the service of God.

Although each local church is shaped by its context, its culture, and its members, they all share the same calling: to glorify God and proclaim the Gospel.

“To the church of God which is at Corinth, to those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints.” (1 Corinthians 1:2)

Let's be honest about a trap of our time: the consumer Christian. He “attends” a church the way you'd go to a restaurant — as long as he likes the program, the worship suits his taste, and the preaching feeds him; at the first disagreement, he goes elsewhere. But the New Testament knows nothing of church spectators: it knows members of a body (1 Corinthians 12:27). A member doesn't “attend” the body; it is part of it. It gives and receives, it carries and is carried. A hand cut off from the body doesn't get to rest: it dies.

The difference shows in the questions you ask. The consumer asks, “What does this church do for me?” The member asks, “What do I bring to this church? Who is expecting me on Sunday? Who would notice if I weren't there? Who is carrying a burden I could share?” This simple reversal changes everything — and it is the path to joy, because Jesus said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

In practice: choose a local church that is faithful to the Bible, commit to it for the long haul, and let yourself be known. It is through consistency and faithfulness — not church-hopping — that the bonds are woven that will be your strength in the day of trial. Roots don't grow in a pot you change every season.

The purpose of local churches

Jesus gave His disciples the foundations of life in a local church: “If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone… For where two or three are gathered together in My name, I am there in the midst of them.” (Matthew 18:15-20)

The first Christians obeyed this teaching by gathering to:

— Proclaim and teach the Word of God.

— Pray and celebrate the Lord's Supper.

— Share brotherly love.

It was also through the life of these local communities that the Gospel spread rapidly in the first century: “Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, labor of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ…” (1 Thessalonians 1:3-10)

Local churches are also where believers learn to live out brotherly love, a powerful witness to the world:

“Love one another. By this all will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:34-35)

titre: The Church — The Problems of Local Churches
texte:
The problems of local churches

The New Testament does not hide the imperfections of local churches:

— Disorder and divisions (1 Corinthians 5:1-5; 1 Corinthians 11:20-22).

— Laziness and abuses (2 Thessalonians 3:6-12).

— False teaching and power struggles (Acts 20:29-30; 1 Corinthians 1:10-13).

The Church is like a spiritual hospital, full of imperfect people in need of Christ's grace and love. Yet, despite their weaknesses, Jesus loves His churches and does not tell us to abandon them:

“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as is the manner of some, but exhorting one another.” (Hebrews 10:25)

If you've been let down by a church, this section is for you. First, that disappointment proves one thing: the Bible told the truth by hiding nothing about the imperfections of communities. Reread the list of New Testament churches: Corinth with its divisions, its lawsuits between brothers, and its scandals; Galatia lured away by a false gospel; Laodicea, lukewarm and self-satisfied (Revelation 3). If Scripture had wanted to sell us an ideal church, it would have buried those files. Instead it lays them out — because the Gospel isn't for the healthy: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark 2:17).

Hold on to the image of the hospital: no one blames a hospital for being full of sick people — that's what it's for. The Church is the hospital of souls: you'll find the wounded, the recovering, the relapses… and the Physician. Anyone looking for a perfect church should ponder the old quip: if you find it, don't join — it would stop being perfect.

Finally, look at Jesus: He was disappointed, betrayed, and denied by His own — and He loved them to the end, and entrusted His Church to those very men. If He didn't abandon His imperfect Church, who are we to do so? That doesn't mean accepting everything: abuses must be named and dealt with — Paul confronted Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11), and Jesus gives a clear process for offenses (Matthew 18:15-17); and if you've been the victim of a church that seriously failed, the path may lead through another community, with help to heal. But between demanding perfection and walking away, there is the way of Christ: loving the Church enough to serve it, rather than judging it from a distance.

titre: The Church — The Organization of Local Churches
texte:
The organization of local churches

Jesus as Head: Jesus is the Chief Shepherd of the universal Church and of local churches.

“Therefore take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, among which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of the Lord which He purchased with His own blood.” (Acts 20:28)

Leaders in the church:

— Pastors: called to guide and feed the flock.

— Elders: watching over the church with devotion and humility (1 Peter 5:1-4).

— Deacons: responsible for practical tasks and mutual care (1 Timothy 3:8-10).

A word of balance on spiritual authority, because our era swings between two extremes. On one side, systematic distrust: recognizing no authority at all, building a pick-and-choose Christianity. On the other, servility: following a man blindly, which has produced many abuses and wounds. The biblical way holds both ends: “Obey those who rule over you, and be submissive, for they watch out for your souls, as those who must give account” (Hebrews 13:17) — AND the Bereans were praised, not blamed, for examining the Scriptures daily “to find out whether these things were so” (Acts 17:11). A clear-eyed trust: we follow shepherds who are themselves under the authority of the Word, and the Word remains the judge of all.

Notice also HOW the Bible describes good leaders: Peter asks the elders to shepherd the flock “not by compulsion but willingly, not for dishonest gain but eagerly; nor as being lords over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2-3). Three “nots” that outline the possible abuses — and the model is Jesus Himself, who knelt to wash His disciples' feet: in His Kingdom, authority is worn like a servant's apron, not like a crown.

A very simple application: pray for your leaders, by name and regularly. They carry a weight few people measure — the burdens of the sheep, the criticism, their own spiritual life to maintain. A church that prays for its shepherds receives better shepherds; and one sincere word of encouragement on a Sunday can sometimes keep a pastor going for an entire season.

Spiritual Gifts

Every Christian receives gifts from the Holy Spirit to build up the church: the church is a body in which every member has a vital role. All believers are called to discover and exercise their gifts in service (1 Corinthians 12).

“And He Himself gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints for the work of ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11-16)

God gives spiritual gifts to believers through the Holy Spirit for the building up of the Church and to serve others. These gifts are mentioned mainly in three key passages: 1 Corinthians 12, Romans 12, and Ephesians 4. Here is a list of the spiritual gifts with their biblical references.

The question everyone asks: how do I discover my gifts? Here is a proven path in four steps. First, serve — you don't discover your gifts sitting down, but by walking; start where there is a need, even a modest one: welcoming, children, tech, meals. Many have discovered a gift of teaching by agreeing to lead a small group, a gift of mercy by visiting someone sick. Second, listen for confirmation: when you exercise your gift, others are built up and tell you so, often before you've seen it yourself. Third, watch for fruit and joy: a gift comes with fruitfulness and a deep sense of “this is what I was made for.” Fourth, ask your elders: they have perspective and the responsibility to help you find your place.

Keep in mind the three key words of 1 Corinthians 12:7: “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each one FOR THE PROFIT OF ALL.” To each one — no one is forgotten, there is no Christian without a gift; given — it is grace, not merit, so neither pride nor jealousy; for the profit of all — a gift is not a personal trophy, it's a tool for service. Whoever says “I have no gift” contradicts the Word; whoever shows off theirs has forgotten what it's for.

And let us restate our conviction, grounded in the Word: these gifts are for today. “Pursue love, and desire spiritual gifts” (1 Corinthians 14:1) — a command never revoked, and notice the pairing Paul makes: love AND gifts, not one without the other. 1 Corinthians 13, the great love chapter, isn't written to replace the gifts but to make them work — it sits between chapters 12 and 14 like the heart between two lungs. The Church needs prophecy, healings, and miracles no less than in the first century; it needs them in a world that doubts God is alive — and it needs them in order and in love.

The Gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:7-11

1. Wisdom — the ability to apply spiritual truths to practical situations with discernment (v. 8).

2. Knowledge — the ability to understand deep truths of God revealed by the Holy Spirit (v. 8).

3. Faith — an exceptional trust in God for extraordinary works (v. 9).

4. Gifts of healing — the ability to heal diseases and restore health by the power of God (v. 9).

5. Miracles — the power to perform supernatural acts to glorify God (v. 10).

6. Prophecy — God-inspired speaking to build up, exhort, and comfort (v. 10).

7. Discerning of spirits — the ability to distinguish between spirits that come from God and those that do not (v. 10).

8. Different kinds of tongues — the gift of speaking in a language one has not learned (v. 10).

9. Interpretation of tongues — the ability to explain the meaning of a tongue given by the Spirit (v. 10).

titre: The Church — The Gifts in Romans 12:6-8 and Ephesians 4:11-13
texte:
The Gifts in Romans 12:6-8 and Ephesians 4:11-13

In Romans 12:6-8:

1. Prophecy — declaring God's truth in proportion to faith (v. 6).

2. Serving — the ability to serve others with diligence and humility (v. 7).

3. Teaching — the ability to convey God's Word with clarity and understanding (v. 7).

4. Exhortation — encouraging, strengthening, and comforting others in their faith (v. 8).

5. Giving — contributing generously to meet the material needs of others (v. 8).

6. Leadership (or administration) — the ability to lead or guide with wisdom and diligence (v. 8).

7. Mercy — the ability to show compassion and empathy toward those who suffer (v. 8).

In Ephesians 4:11-13:

1. Apostles — those sent to establish the Church, especially in new territories (v. 11).

2. Prophets — those who declare God's truth under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit (v. 11).

3. Evangelists — those who share the Gospel and bring people to Christ (v. 11).

4. Pastors — those who care spiritually for God's flock, guiding and protecting them (v. 11).

5. Teachers — those who instruct believers in biblical doctrine (v. 11).

Specific gifts mentioned in other passages:

— Celibacy (1 Corinthians 7:7) — a God-given ability to serve without being distracted by the responsibilities of marriage.

— Hospitality (1 Peter 4:9-10) — the ability to welcome others with generosity and love.

— Intercession — though not listed as a spiritual gift, some people are especially called to pray fervently for others (James 5:16).

For Reflection

1. The model of the church: the Church is often compared to a family, a team, an army, or a body. What do these images reveal about the nature and role of the church?

2. Your place in the church: how do you see yourself in the body of Christ? What role and what gifts are you putting to work in service?

3. Your spiritual gifts: what gifts has the Holy Spirit entrusted to you, and how are you using them to build up your local church?

The church is much more than an institution: it is a living community, loved by God and destined to reflect His love in the world.

Conclusion

The Church, whether universal or local, is much more than a simple gathering or a human organization: it is a living community, the bride of Christ, and the spiritual body of which Jesus is the head.

The universal Church transcends borders and cultures, bringing together all who have put their faith in Jesus Christ. Local churches, for their part, embody this universal reality in specific settings, where believers gather to glorify God, proclaim the Gospel, and live out brotherly love.

Despite their imperfections, local churches are where Christians grow spiritually, exercise their gifts, and find support and encouragement. They are called to reflect God's love in the world and to become beacons of light and hope.

As believers, each of us is called to play an active role in the Church, to discover and use our gifts for building up the body of Christ, and to persevere in fellowship despite the challenges. The Church is a living testimony to the grace, love, and glory of God, and each of us has a unique and essential place in this magnificent spiritual building.

“But, speaking the truth in love, may grow up in all things into Him who is the head—Christ—from whom the whole body, joined and knit together by what every joint supplies, according to the effective working by which every part does its share, causes growth of the body for the edifying of itself in love.” (Ephesians 4:15-16)

titre: The Christian's New Life — The Model of the Early Church
texte:
The Model of the Early Church

To build a Church that reflects God's will as fully as possible, we draw on the example of the early Church described in the book of Acts.

“And they continued steadfastly in the apostles' teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers.” (Acts 2:42)

These four foundational areas are essential in the Christian life. They reflect a deep commitment to God and to His community.

These four pillars — teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer — are like the four legs of a table: remove one, and everything wobbles. A Christian who is all teaching but no fellowship becomes a head without a body; all fellowship but no teaching, a heart without a backbone; without prayer, an engine without fuel.

The verb Luke chose deserves attention: they continued steadfastly. The Greek word, proskartereō, describes tenacious constancy, a faithfulness that holds on — the same word describes the disciples in prayer before Pentecost. Not “they tried when they had time”: they held fast, consistently. It's a marathon word, not a sprint word. Yet ours is an age of short-lived enthusiasm: we start everything and stick with little. The Christian life isn't built on flashes of brilliance, but on faithfulness — next Sunday's service, tomorrow morning's reading, tonight's prayer. God does wonders with ordinary people who don't let go.

And look at the result of that perseverance, two verses later: “fear came upon every soul… they ate their food with gladness… and the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved” (Acts 2:43-47). Growth wasn't a strategy: it was the overflow of a healthy community. Take care of the four pillars; God takes care of the harvest.

titre: The Christian's New Life — The Apostles' Teaching
texte:
The Apostles' Teaching

In New Testament times, baptism marked conversion and entry into the Church. New believers were immediately immersed in the apostles' teaching, that is, in the knowledge of God's Word.

However, many Christians today neglect teaching and doctrine, thinking they are secondary to spiritual experience or emotion. Yet a Christian without solid biblical teaching is like a house without a foundation or a body without a skeleton. He is at risk of wavering in the face of spiritual fads or false doctrines.

Jesus Himself gave teaching an important place: “Teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:20)

Solid biblical teaching doesn't divide; it helps us discern between the essential and the secondary, remain faithful to the truth, and avoid cults. This teaching is found today in the Bible, the inspired Word of God.

Let's get practical: how do you feed on the Word when you're just starting out? Here's a simple method that has helped thousands of Christians. Choose a set time — consistency matters more than length: fifteen minutes every day is better than two hours once a month. Start with a Gospel, Mark or John, rather than Genesis (many get bogged down in Leviticus trying to read everything in order). Read a short passage, then ask it three questions: What does it show me about God? What does it reveal about me? What will I put into practice today? Write one sentence in your journal, and finish with a short prayer responding to what you read.

Jesus told a parable that shows what's at stake: two men build similar houses; the storm comes — the same storm for both; one stands, the other collapses. The difference wasn't visible in good weather: it was in the foundations. And Jesus specifies: the rock is “whoever hears these sayings of Mine, AND DOES THEM” (Matthew 7:24). Not just hearing: doing. The Word read but not lived produces fragile scholars; the Word practiced produces houses that stand. Ask yourself each day not “What did I learn?” but “What am I doing with what I read?”

Psalm 1 paints the portrait of the person nourished by the Word: “a tree planted by the rivers of water, that brings forth its fruit in its season, whose leaf also shall not wither.” Notice: planted — not set down, but rooted over time; by the rivers — the freshness comes from outside, not from the tree; in its season — fruit takes time, and that's normal. The RHEMA app is designed to help you with this: reading plans give you a daily appointment, and the journal keeps track of what God shows you.

titre: The Christian's New Life — The Bible: The Word of God
texte:
The Bible: The Word of God

The Bible, made up of 66 books written over about 15 centuries, is a divine revelation passed on by men inspired by the Holy Spirit.

“All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.” (2 Timothy 3:16-17)

Regular contact with the Bible, whether through reading, meditation, or study, is indispensable. These moments allow God to speak to us, transform us, instruct us, and nourish our faith.

“As newborn babes, desire the pure milk of the word, that you may grow thereby.” (1 Peter 2:2)

Let's take the measure of this book: 66 books, some forty authors — shepherds, kings, fishermen, doctors, prophets — three languages, three continents, fifteen centuries of writing… and one coherent story, from the garden of Genesis to the city of Revelation, entirely centered on one person: Jesus Christ. It's as if forty musicians, separated by centuries and knowing nothing of one another, had each composed one movement — and in the end, the whole formed a perfect symphony. There is one Composer behind the musicians: that is what inspiration means.

Jesus Himself shows us what to do with this book. In the wilderness, facing the tempter, He doesn't argue or philosophize: three times He answers, “It is written” (Matthew 4). The One who was the living Word fought with the written Word — what more could we need? That's why Paul calls Scripture “the sword of the Spirit” (Ephesians 6:17): the only offensive weapon in the Christian's whole armor. A sheathed sword protects no one: memorize verses — start with one a week — and you'll have steel in hand on the day of temptation.

One last watchword: the Bible isn't a book to defend; it's a book to open. As one preacher put it: “Defend the Bible? You might as well defend a lion — open the cage and it will defend itself.” Your part isn't to win debates about Scripture, but to read it, live it, and help others taste it.

Fellowship

Fellowship, mentioned right after the apostles' teaching, holds a central place in the Christian life. It isn't limited to friendly relationships, shared opinions, or a pleasant atmosphere. It runs much deeper:

— A spiritual union through the Holy Spirit: believers, indwelt by the same Spirit, are members of one spiritual family (Ephesians 4:25).

— Fellowship with God and with the brethren: being in fellowship with God is the foundation of true fellowship with one another (1 John 1:3).

Fellowship shows itself through: attention to others' needs, generosity and hospitality, and participation in gatherings, prayer, and shared meals.

“They ate their food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved.” (Acts 2:46-47)

It brings comfort and encouragement, especially in trials, and is a powerful testimony to those who don't know Jesus.

Here's a simple test to gauge your fellowship: what do you talk about after the service? If our church conversations stop at the weather and “How are you? — Fine,” we're a waiting room, not a family. Fellowship begins when we dare to be truthful: asking for prayer for a real battle, confessing a struggle, sharing a deep joy.

The New Testament is full of commands you simply can't live out alone — theologians call them the “one anothers”: love one another, bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2), exhort one another daily (Hebrews 3:13), confess your sins to one another and pray for one another (James 5:16), forgive one another… About fifty occurrences. Try obeying just one of these commands alone on your couch: impossible. God designed Christian growth as a team sport.

That's why large gatherings aren't enough: in a big assembly you listen; in a small circle, you're known. Both are needed, like the public square and the kitchen table. In practical terms: join a home group or find a prayer partner — someone you can text at eleven at night, someone who has the right to ask you the uncomfortable questions. Ecclesiastes put it plainly: “Two are better than one… For if they fall, one will lift up his companion. But woe to him who is alone when he falls, for he has no one to help him up.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10).

titre: The Christian's New Life — The Breaking of Bread and Prayer
texte:
The Breaking of Bread and Prayer

The breaking of bread: this topic was covered in the lesson on the Lord's Supper.

Prayer: “Pray without ceasing.” (1 Thessalonians 5:17)

Prayer isn't merely reciting words, but a sincere conversation with God, a dialogue between a child and their heavenly Father, a constant connection. Someone has said: prayer is the breath of the soul.

Jesus Himself gave us the example: “But you, when you pray, go into your room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in the secret place.” (Matthew 6:6)

Christian prayer is empowered by the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:26). It includes adoration, praise, confession, thanksgiving, intercession, and even spiritual warfare.

For those who don't know where to start in prayer, here is a simple, easy-to-remember structure in four movements: adoration — telling God who He is, praising Him for His character; repentance — honestly confessing to Him what needs confessing; thanksgiving — thanking Him for the concrete blessings of the day; requests — bringing Him needs, your own and those of others. A few minutes are enough to begin. It isn't a magic formula: it's a marked trail so the conversation doesn't go in circles — exactly what Jesus did when He gave the Lord's Prayer to His disciples who asked, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1). Notice, by the way, the order of the Lord's Prayer: God's name, kingdom, and will first, our needs next. Prayer begins by lifting our eyes before opening our hands.

And let's free ourselves from a false idea: prayer isn't a performance reserved for “spiritual” moments, nor a matter of fine phrases. Jesus warns: “When you pray, do not use vain repetitions… your Father knows the things you have need of before you ask Him” (Matthew 6:7-8). Look at the prayers that run through Scripture: “Lord, save me!” (Peter sinking, three words), “Remember me” (the thief), “Your will be done” (Jesus in Gethsemane). Short, real, bare. God prefers three sincere words to three hours of recitation.

“Pray without ceasing” then becomes possible: not staying on your knees endlessly, but living in continual conversation with an ever-present Father — while driving, walking, facing a difficult file, before a delicate conversation. Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia, gives a lightning-quick example: between the king's question and his own answer, the text notes, “So I prayed to the God of heaven. And I said to the king” (Nehemiah 2:4-5) — a one-second silent prayer between two sentences. That is the breath of the soul.

titre: The Christian's New Life — Being a Disciple of Jesus: A Visible and Verbal Witness
texte:
Being a Disciple of Jesus: A Visible and Verbal Witness

The life of the first Christians was radically different from that of the world. People recognized that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13). Jesus had warned that His disciples would be persecuted, because the world does not love those who remind it of its own corruption (2 Timothy 3:12; John 16:33).

The Christian is called to share the Gospel, not only through his life, but also through his words:

“Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you.” (Matthew 28:19-20)

Every Christian is a missionary in daily life, a witness to the grace of God.

Witnessing feels intimidating as long as you think you have to be a theologian. But biblical witness is within everyone's reach: it's telling your story. The man born blind who was healed in John 9 is summoned by the religious experts, who bombard him with theological questions he can't answer — and he responds with the one thing no one can dispute: “Whether He is a sinner or not I do not know. One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see.” The whole room of experts is left speechless. No one can argue with your story — it's yours.

Prepare it in three parts; two minutes is enough: my life before, my encounter with Jesus, what has changed since. That is exactly the structure Paul uses before King Agrippa (Acts 26): his life as a persecutor, the road to Damascus, his life since. Write it down, say it out loud once to get comfortable with it — and it will be ready the day a conversation opens up. And conversations will open up: Peter asks us to be “always ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you” — and he adds the manner: “with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15-16). No pressure, no contempt: a hope that shows, and a gentle answer when people ask.

Finally, remember this very simple approach: invite rather than convince. When Nathanael scoffs — “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” — Philip doesn't start a debate: he says, “Come and see” (John 1:46). The Samaritan woman does the same with her whole village: “Come, see a Man who told me all things that I ever did” (John 4:29) — and the village comes. You don't have to win a debate; you can open a door: an invitation to a service, to a meal, to go through a reading plan together, often bears more fruit than a thousand arguments.

titre: The Christian's New Life — Being a Disciple of Jesus: How We Use Our Possessions and Our Time
texte:
Being a Disciple of Jesus: How We Use Our Possessions and Our Time

How we use our possessions: money and material possessions are sensitive areas, but Jesus taught that we are stewards of what God entrusts to us.

“You are not your own, for you were bought at a price.” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20)

From the very beginning, believers understood the importance of giving to God with gratitude (Genesis 4; 14:20).

How we use our time: time, like money, belongs to God. The Christian is invited to devote every moment to the glory of God, whether at work, at leisure, or in worship.

“So teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” (Psalms 90:12)

“See then that you walk circumspectly, not as fools but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” (Ephesians 5:15-16)

A revealing exercise to do once: the one-week audit. For seven days, honestly write down the time spent on screens, then the time spent in the Word and in prayer. The result is often a healthy wake-up call — not to make you feel guilty, but to help you choose: we don't lack time; we've already given it to something else. Redeeming the time means deliberately taking it back for what matters. Moses turned this into a prayer: “So teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (Psalms 90:12) — numbering our days means remembering that they are numbered; and it's that remembrance that makes us wise.

As for possessions, Jesus told the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30): a master entrusts his goods to his servants — to each according to his ability — and then goes away. Two servants make them grow; the third buries his talent out of fear and gives back to the master exactly what he received, intact and fruitless. Notice: he stole nothing, wasted nothing — he simply did nothing. And he's the one the master rebukes. The parable turns our caution upside down: in God's eyes, the risk isn't giving too much; it's burying. Everything you have — money, time, talents, relationships — has been entrusted to you to produce something, not to be stored underground.

The biblical image is that of the steward: a manager to whom the master has entrusted his house during his absence. The steward lives in the house and enjoys it, but never says “it's mine” — and he knows that one day he will give an account. Living this way frees us from money's two tyrannies: greed, which clings to it, and anxiety, which fears it. Everything belongs to God; I manage, He provides — “Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matthew 6:33).

Conclusion

The Christian's new life is a radical and ongoing transformation, marked by deep communion with God and a renewed relationship with others. It rests on essential pillars: the Word of God, prayer, fellowship, and witness.

Following the example of the first Christians, every believer is called to persevere in love, faith, and service, while reflecting the light of Christ in a world in need of salvation.

This transformed life is not limited to spiritual practices; it also touches how we use our possessions, our time, and our resources, through faithful stewardship centered on the glory of God. Being a disciple of Jesus involves self-denial, a visible and verbal witness, and total dependence on God's grace.

So the Christian's new life bears witness to God's work in him, driving him to grow in spiritual maturity and to take an active part in advancing the Kingdom of God. This life is a path of joyful surrender to God's will, bringing lasting peace and a joy that rises above circumstances.

“I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

titre: God Looks at the Heart — Introduction and Context
texte:
Introduction

David, an incredible destiny. The little shepherd boy nobody noticed, forgotten out in the fields among the sheep, became the greatest king of Israel. Why him? Not because he was the tallest, the strongest, or the most handsome. God chose him for one reason only: his heart.

We live in a society where image is king, more and more every day. People judge you by your looks, your clothes, your followers, the brand of your phone. But I have good news for you: God hasn't changed. While the world looks at your outside, God looks at your heart.

Today, we're going to understand something that can change your life:

The Lord does not see as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.

(1 Samuel 16:7)

Background

Israel was going through a deep transition. Until then, the people had no king like the other nations. God led them through judges and prophets, and Samuel had become one of the most important figures of that period. Yet as he grew old, Samuel appointed his sons as judges, but they did not walk in his ways. They pursued their own interests, took bribes, and perverted justice.

So the elders of Israel came to Samuel with a request: “Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5). This request deeply displeased Samuel, but God explained that it wasn't really him they were rejecting: “They have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me, that I should not reign over them” (1 Samuel 8:7). The people now wanted a visible king, a man who would go out before them, lead their armies, and make them look like the other nations.

Samuel warned them of the consequences of such a choice. He explained that a king would take their sons for his army, their daughters for his service, and part of their land, their harvests, and their possessions. Despite this, the people refused to change their minds. They wanted a king, and God allowed it to happen.

Keep this starting point in mind: Israel isn't looking for the king God wants, but for a king who will look good next to the other nations. Everything else in the story flows from there.

titre: God Looks at the Heart — Saul, the Man the People Chose
texte:
Saul, the Man the People Chose

Before David, there was Saul.

It is in this context that Saul appears. From his very first appearance in the biblical account, Saul is described as an impressive man: “a choice and handsome young man. There was not a more handsome person than he among the children of Israel. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people” (1 Samuel 9:2). In human eyes, he looked exactly like what you'd expect a king to look like. He had the stature, the presence, and the bearing.

One day, his father's donkeys got lost, and Kish sent Saul to look for them with a servant. They went through several regions without finding them. Just as they were about to head home, the servant suggested that Saul go consult a man of God who lived nearby. That man was Samuel. But Saul didn't know that God had already prepared this meeting. The day before, God had told Samuel that a man from the tribe of Benjamin would come to him and that he was to anoint him as leader of His people. When Saul arrived, Samuel immediately understood that this was the man God had spoken about. After welcoming him, he took him aside, and the next day he poured oil on his head to establish him as leader of the people.

Samuel gave him several signs to confirm that this call truly came from God, and he also told him that the Spirit of God would come upon him. That's exactly what happened. Saul was seized by the Spirit, he prophesied, and the Bible even says that “God gave him another heart” (1 Samuel 10:9).

And on paper, Saul had it all. The people were proud: finally, a king who looks the part! The people looked at the outside, and the outside was perfect. Except that behind this beautiful image was a man who would become a very bad king.

The Real Portrait of Saul

A good start

titre: God Looks at the Heart — Saul Disobeys
texte:
At the beginning, Saul doesn't seem to be a proud man. When he realizes Samuel is talking to him about a royal destiny, he points out that he belongs to Benjamin, “the smallest of the tribes of Israel,” and that his family is “the least of all” (1 Samuel 9:21). Later, when he is to be presented publicly to the people, he even hides among the baggage (1 Samuel 10:22). They have to go get him and bring him before all Israel. When he finally appears, his great height immediately catches everyone's eye, and the people acclaim him as king.

Saul's beginnings are encouraging. When an Israelite city is threatened by the Ammonites, the Spirit of God comes powerfully upon him (1 Samuel 11:6). Saul gathers the people, leads the army into battle, and wins a major victory. His position then seems firmly established. He has authority, the people's support, military victories, and above all, he has experienced the work of the Spirit of God in his life.

A disobedient man (1 Samuel 13:8-14)

He despised the law of the Lord: “You have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God, which He commanded you” (1 Samuel 13:13)

Yet little by little, something begins to deteriorate in his heart. The first major turning point comes during a conflict with the Philistines. Samuel had asked him to wait for him so that he could offer a sacrifice to the Lord before the battle. The enemy army is impressive, the Israelites are afraid, and several soldiers start deserting. When Saul sees his men scattering and Samuel is late, he decides to act on his own. He offers the burnt offering without waiting for the prophet.

No sooner is the sacrifice finished than Samuel arrives. When he asks him what he has done, Saul immediately starts justifying himself. He explains that the people were scattering, that the Philistines were ready to attack, and that Samuel hadn't come when expected: “Therefore I felt compelled, and offered a burnt offering” (1 Samuel 13:12). Saul let the pressure of the situation become stronger than his obedience to God's word.

Samuel then tells him that his kingdom will not continue: “The Lord has sought for Himself a man after His own heart” (1 Samuel 13:14). God is already announcing that another man will come after Saul.

He cared more about people's opinion than God's: “I feared the people and obeyed their voice” (1 Samuel 15:24)

titre: God Looks at the Heart — Saul Rejected as King
texte:
A little later, Saul disobeys again in an even clearer way. God gives him a mission against Amalek and, through Samuel, gives him precise instructions. Saul goes to battle and wins, but he doesn't fully carry out what he was told. He spares Agag, the king of Amalek, and keeps the best animals and everything he considers valuable (1 Samuel 15:9).

God then speaks to Samuel and tells him that Saul has turned away from Him and has not kept His word. Samuel is deeply grieved and spends the night crying out to God. The next day, when he meets Saul, Saul greets him by claiming he has carried out God's word. Yet Samuel hears the sound of the sheep that were kept and asks him what this bleating means. Once again, Saul starts justifying himself. He explains that the people kept the best animals to offer them as sacrifices to God.

That's when Samuel reminds him of an essential truth: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). He tells him that because he has rejected the word of God, God has in turn rejected him as king.

He made rash decisions: he made his exhausted army swear not to eat anything until evening (1 Samuel 14:24)

A man who didn't keep his word: he swore that his own son Jonathan would die, and the people had to rescue him (1 Samuel 14:44-45)

Willing to do anything to keep his throne: he would spend his life trying to kill David (1 Samuel 18:11)

It's important to understand that the text doesn't simply present God as having stopped loving Saul. What is rejected here is his position as king. Saul had received a responsibility, authority, and a mission, but his repeated refusal to obey had deeply marked his reign.

As Samuel turns to leave, Saul grabs his robe, and it tears. Samuel immediately uses this as a prophetic sign: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today, and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you” (1 Samuel 15:28).

After this episode, Samuel keeps mourning over Saul. He is deeply affected by what happened. But one day, God says to him: “How long will you mourn for Saul? […] Fill your horn with oil, and go; I am sending you to Jesse the Bethlehemite. For I have provided Myself a king among his sons” (1 Samuel 16:1).

The perfect portrait of a king, at least on the outside. A huge failure in reality. He lived his life without ever submitting to God, he disobeyed again and again, and he never truly repented. A great start, a horrible ending, and God rejected him.

titre: God Looks at the Heart — Application: The Trap of Appearances
texte:
What This Says to Us

Many people start well. They get saved, give their lives to the Lord, and then, over time, they grow cold, make compromises, let sin in, and end up leaving the church. And on the flip side, others had a horrible past, marked by suffering, and along the way they find the Lord and see their lives completely restored.

It's never the starting point that matters most, it's the heart. God is ready to welcome you with open arms and rebuild you, as long as your heart is sincere. That's why the Bible says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it spring the issues of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

The Trap of Appearances

Look closely at this detail: at the moment God rejects him, Saul still has the chance to repent. He does say, “I have sinned,” but right away he adds: “please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel” (1 Samuel 15:30). His only concern is his image in front of the people. His image! To the very end, he preferred to save face rather than save his heart.

And sometimes we're exactly the same. We let ourselves be impressed by what we see, when appearances are often deceiving.

We want so badly to impress others. We go on a trip, and in front of a gorgeous view, before we even look at it, we pull out our phone for the photo and the post: “dream vacation.” Nothing against photos; the problem is the motivation behind them. We no longer enjoy the moment, we stage it.

Why do we want so badly to impress others?

Often, quite simply, because we don't love ourselves enough. And someone who doesn't love themselves can neither love nor feel loved.

Because we're not sure of our worth. We feel like without the right sneakers or the right phone, we're nobody.

Because we want to be loved. So we pretend to be what we're not.

I know it's hard to be young today, and even harder to be a young Christian. But I promise you one thing: living under the yoke of appearances is much worse. Always having to wear the latest trend; constantly comparing yourself; living on a diet to look like models who eat one carrot for breakfast. We're never satisfied: I'm too fat, too skinny, too tall, too short, my hair is too this, not enough that. Pretending in front of others about the way we think and act, all to please people. Real bondage.

titre: God Looks at the Heart — Your Worth Is in Jesus
texte:
Your Worth Is in Jesus

How do you love yourself? Your worth isn't found in your job, your looks, a nice house, a big car, designer clothes, or the latest phone. Your worth doesn't depend on how others see you. You'll never win everyone over. Even Jesus didn't: during His time on earth, He experienced more rejection than approval. So don't measure your worth by other people's opinions.

Your worth is in Jesus Christ. Because He's the only one who sees you as you really are and loves you for who you are. With your flaws, your morning breath, your messy hair, and the little love handles you try to hide. He loves you just like that. And He loved you first: “We love Him because He first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

And here's what's amazing: when you understand Jesus' love and feel loved by Him, you're finally able to love yourself. And when you love yourself as you are, strangely enough, others love you too. Because “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18): someone who knows they're loved by God is no longer afraid of rejection, and becomes free to love in return.

Stop doing everything to get people to love you. Seek the perfect love of Jesus instead. That love will give you confidence, and with that confidence you learn to accept yourself. And if some people reject you, it doesn't hurt you. God created you exactly as you are, and His Word says you are “fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalms 139:14). Whoever despises someone despises the God who created them.

(1 John 4:18)

titre: God Looks at the Heart — David, the Man God Chose
texte:
David, the Man God Chose

Now, look at how God chooses.

So Samuel goes to Bethlehem. When he arrives, the elders of the town come trembling to meet him: “Do you come peaceably?” (1 Samuel 16:4). The arrival of a prophet of his stature could just as easily signal a blessing as a judgment. Samuel reassures them and invites them to consecrate themselves to take part in a sacrifice. Jesse and his sons are invited as well.

When Jesse's first son steps before Samuel, his name is Eliab. Tall, imposing, a true warrior. His appearance impresses Samuel so much that he immediately thinks, “Surely this is the one!” But God stops him and teaches him something fundamental. He tells him not to look at this man's appearance or his height, because people look at what strikes the eye, while God looks at the heart.

These words hit even harder when you remember Saul. Saul had been exactly the kind of man who caught everyone's eye because of his stature. He stood head and shoulders above everyone else. But now God wants to teach Samuel that He doesn't choose by the same standards as people. So Jesse has his sons pass before Samuel one after another. Each time, God's answer is the same: not this one. Seven sons pass before the prophet, but none of them is the one God has chosen.

Do not look at his appearance or at his physical stature, because I have refused him. For the Lord does not see as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.

(1 Samuel 16:7)

A portrait of David

A despised child, not even invited to the sacrifice by his own family (1 Samuel 16:11)

A shepherd, the least prestigious job of his time

titre: God Looks at the Heart — The Anointing of David
texte:
An ancient Jewish tradition suggests that David grew up under the suspicion of being an illegitimate child (in Hebrew, a “mamzer”), which would partly explain why he seems to have been sidelined within his own family. The Bible never says so explicitly, but some passages point toward this exclusion.

**His role in the family:** David was a shepherd, probably the most despised job of the time. Jesse had eight sons (1 Samuel 17:12), and David was the only shepherd. On top of that, a shepherd lived mostly out in the fields, not in the house with everyone else.

**David was treated differently from his brothers:** when Samuel comes to Jesse's house to anoint the future king, Jesse presents seven of his sons, while David is left outside with the sheep. Samuel even has to ask, “Are all the young men here?” before Jesse admits, “There remains yet the youngest, and there he is, keeping the sheep” (1 Samuel 16:11).

**Family rejection and hostility:** David later writes, “I have become a stranger to my brothers, and an alien to my mother's children” (Psalms 69:8), the memory of a deep family rejection. His brother Eliab's hostility also shows up when David arrives at the battlefield: Eliab gets angry with him, belittles his work as a shepherd, and accuses him of pride: “I know your pride and the insolence of your heart” (1 Samuel 17:28).

**Psalm 51:** “Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me” (Psalms 51:5). Many read this first as a confession of the sinful nature of every human being; others also see in it the echo of this childhood wound.

But a man of valor, well-spoken, with fine manners (1 Samuel 16:18)

Above all, a man who walked with God: “the Lord is with him” (1 Samuel 16:18)

And a tender heart: an artist, a musician whose harp soothed Saul (1 Samuel 16:23). Worship and spiritual life

So Samuel finally turns to Jesse and asks him if he has another son. Jesse answers that the youngest is still left, but he's outside keeping the sheep. That detail is especially striking. When Samuel had asked to see Jesse's sons, David hadn't even been called. He had stayed in the fields, busy watching his father's flock. Samuel then asks for someone to go get him and says they won't go on until he arrives.

So they go get David from the fields. The young shepherd walks into the house and stands before Samuel. At that moment, God speaks clearly to the prophet: “Arise, anoint him; for this is the one!” (1 Samuel 16:12). Samuel takes the horn of oil he had brought and pours the oil on David's head, in the midst of his brothers. From that day on, the Spirit of the Lord came upon David (1 Samuel 16:13).

This moment is extraordinary, because on the surface nothing has changed yet. Saul is still sitting on the throne. He still has the palace, the army, and the crown. David has no kingdom and no soldiers. He's still just a young shepherd from Bethlehem. And yet something essential has just shifted in the spiritual realm. The one nobody thought to call has just been chosen by God.

Through human eyes, David had none of what it takes to be king. Too young, no experience, just a guy watching sheep. It's as if someone told you today that the next president would be a high school kid with no diploma. Or a young garbage collector with no education. Unthinkable! And yet David became Israel's greatest king, the one from whom Jesus Himself would descend.

titre: God Looks at the Heart — Application: God Looks at the Inside
texte:
Because God looks at the inside

And that changes everything for you:

God has a plan bigger than your past.

Many young people drag their past around like a ball and chain and don't dare move forward; they don't feel worthy. But “there is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). In Christ, your sins are wiped away, and your life starts over from scratch.

God has a plan bigger than your limitations.

You don't feel capable? Not qualified enough? David is proof that God makes you capable. He's the one who gives you strength, gifts, and the right people along your path.

God plans a season of preparation.

David was trained in the fields before he was crowned. It was while keeping the sheep that he learned to fight the lion and the bear, to play the harp, and to talk with God. God doesn't throw you into the deep end without preparing you first.

God opens doors you think are shut.

“There's no way I could ever become that… no way I'll find the right person…” We forget that we have the God of the impossible.

God doesn't choose you because of what you are, because otherwise no one would qualify: we're all sinners, all full of shortcomings. He looks at you from His own perspective. Now it's your turn to look at your future through the eyes of faith.

And what about your decisions?

Be careful, because when appearance becomes important to you, it ends up dictating your choices. And a decision based on appearance leads you straight to failure, because appearance is like smoke: it fades away and gives way to reality.

As a young person, you have huge decisions to make:

Your path, your studies, your career:

if you choose for prestige or for money, one day you'll wake up unhappy, feeling like you've wasted your life.

Your future wife, your future husband:

if you choose based on looks alone, you may end up next to someone you have nothing to share with.

Your friends:

if you choose them for what they can give you, you build self-serving relationships where you can't even be yourself.

The people of Israel chose their king based on appearance. The consequences were terrible. Don't make the same mistake with your life.

titre: God Looks at the Heart — Conclusion, Questions, and Prayer
texte:
Conclusion and application

God has an extraordinary destiny for each of you. And the only thing He's looking for is a heart turned toward Him, a sincere heart. He'll take care of the rest.

Youth is one of the most beautiful seasons of life. It's also when you make the most important decisions, often without feeling ready. You have a thousand questions. You don't have a manual with all the answers ready-made.

But here's the first clue: God looks at your heart. He looks at your motives. So lay your life before Him. Even when you don't do everything perfectly, He knows your heart. If you trust Him, if you let Him guide your life, He will show you the way. Not the world's idea of success, but joy, peace, true happiness: the kind you find when you do what you were created for.

Commit your way to the Lord, trust also in Him, and He shall bring it to pass.

(Psalms 37:5)

People look at appearance; God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

Saul looked like a king but cared more about his image than about obedience; David had nothing going for him, but his heart was turned toward God.

Your worth doesn't depend on what others think of you: it's found in Jesus, who loves you just as you are.

Don't make your big decisions based on appearance: ask God to guide your heart.

In what areas of your life are you most impressed by appearance (social media, looks, comparing yourself to others)?

Honestly: are you more focused on being liked by people, or on understanding that Jesus already loves you just as you are?

Is there a “past” or a “limitation” keeping you from believing God can use you? What does Romans 8:1 say to that?

Every morning, before you look at your phone, read Psalm 139:14 out loud and remember who you are in God's eyes.

I will praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made; marvelous are Your works, and my soul knows it very well.

(Psalms 139:14)

Lord, thank You for not looking at me the way others do. You know my heart, with its wounds and its shortcomings, and You love me anyway. Forgive me for the times I tried to impress instead of obeying You. Teach me to find my worth in You alone, and keep my heart turned toward You in all my decisions. In Jesus' name, amen.

To go further this week

(1 Samuel 16:1-13)

David anointed

(1 Samuel 15:10-31)

Saul rejected as king

(Psalms 139:1-18)

God knows me and formed me

(1 John 4:7-19)

Perfect love casts out fear

(Romans 8:1-17)

No condemnation, children of God
